recruits.name: Dan Okafor
recruits.backstory: Twenty-two years on a Sheffield steel floor. Heat, noise, a four-man crew and the kind of trust you can't talk about without sounding daft. Then the plant shut. Then the world ended, which he'll tell you came as less of a shock than the first one. He's a shield. That's the whole arrangement. He stands in front and the rest of you get on with it.
recruits.greeting: I'll go first, and there's no need to thank me for it. It's the job, and somebody has to have it.
recruits.home_note: At the drill grounds in Valley of Strength.

background_sections.before: Dan worked a steel floor in Sheffield for twenty-two years, in the heat and the noise with a crew of four men. They trusted each other in a way he can't describe without sounding daft, and they went for a pint every Friday for nine years straight. Then the plant closed in 2019, and he was out of work for four years. He'll walk away from you if you ask him about those four years. His daughter lived in Leeds, and he saw her less than he should have.
background_sections.adjustment: He'll tell you he got used to this world the day he stopped being idle, and that was the whole of it. He's wrong about that, but he's wrong in a direction that works for him. After four years with nothing to do, having a job again mattered more to him than which world it was on. He says the end of the world came as less of a shock than the plant closing.
background_sections.now: He lives in Orgrimmar, near the forges, in a bunk he keeps very tidy, because the heat and the hammering feel like home. He takes the front of whatever goes out, and in three years he's never asked to be paid differently for it. He's a shield, and that's the whole arrangement. He stands in front and everyone else gets on with it.
background_sections.forward: Dan wants a crew again, four men, long shifts and a pint on a Friday. He's been putting one together out of whoever's in the tavern, and it isn't the same, and he won't say so. The lists of the missing in Orgrimmar are alphabetical, and he's read his way to his daughter's surname about forty times. He keeps going back.

recruits.name: Ama Boateng
recruits.backstory: There's a rule about her hours and everybody in Razor Hill knows she breaks it. Twice now the orc women have walked her back to her own cot with a hand between her shoulder blades. She was a children's nurse somewhere with four cots to a bay and an arithmetic nobody said out loud, and what she carried over wasn't the healing. It was the arithmetic. She still runs it, every time, on a world that doesn't make her.
recruits.greeting: Sit down, please, and I mean right now. You're dripping on a floor I've already cleaned once today.
recruits.home_note: Set up in the infirmary tent.

background_sections.before: Ama grew up in Peckham, in south London, above her dad's phone shop, with her little brother Kofi. Her mum was a nurse from Lagos, so Ama became one too, and she spent fourteen years working nights on a children's ward. There were four cots to a bay and never enough nurses, and a ward sister taught her to keep her voice level while her hands did something frightening. She was very good at the job. It cost her a marriage to a man called Kwame and most of her twenties, and she'll tell you the trade was worth it.
background_sections.adjustment: She landed in Durotar still in her uniform, and she doesn't talk about the first two years. Back home there was always a form, a referral or a reason she couldn't help someone. Here there was light in her hands and nothing to stop her, so for a whole year she healed until she fell over and then got up and did it again. In the end an orc woman called Shenra, whose son Ama had kept breathing, picked her up off the floor and told her to stop.
background_sections.now: She runs the infirmary at Razor Hill, where the road brings in whatever the Barrens did to people that week. She heals the worst first, and she makes no apology for it. The orc children stopped being frightened of her a long time after the adults did, and she thinks that's the right way round. She still wears the little bear she clipped to her stethoscope so the children back home would let her listen to their chests.
background_sections.forward: Ama needs someone who can run the infirmary when she's out of the room, a real replacement and not a student. She's been looking for two years and has turned down four people for reasons she can't put into words, and she knows that's the real problem. She keeps a notebook of every child she's lost, by first name, in handwriting nobody else can read. She checks the lists for her dad and Kofi, and she doesn't talk about it.

recruits.name: Silas Vance
recruits.backstory: Ask what he did before and you'll get a different answer each time, all of them port work, none of them checkable. What's true is that he reads a dock the way other people read a face. Which crate's light, which captain's lying, who's about to be robbed by the man standing next to him. He sells that at a fair price and it still faintly embarrasses him. He arrived expecting a free-for-all: no record, no reputation, nothing to live down. What he found was a frontier with sharper rules than Antwerp ever had, because out here the people who break them don't get a hearing. Took four months to understand and it reorganised him completely.
recruits.greeting: You want someone who hits things, or someone who hits things first? They're different rates. I'll quote you the second and do the first, and I'll call it a discount.
recruits.home_note: At the docks, leaning on a crate like he owns it.

background_sections.before:
Five years of cargo manifests and camera feeds at the Port of Antwerp, and the dockside arrangement where everybody took a little and nobody took enough to become a problem.

He didn't join in, and he didn't report it either. Ask him what he believed in back then and he'd have changed the subject, quickly.

There's nobody he's looking for, he says. He mentions that more often than a man who meant it would.
background_sections.adjustment: He landed delighted. He's embarrassed about that now in a way he wouldn't have predicted.
background_sections.now:
Ratchet. A port. The only shape of place he's ever been able to read properly.

There's a goblin on the middle pier paying him a retainer not to tell anyone else what he notices. Silas considers it the single most legitimate income of his life.
background_sections.forward:
A berth. Not ownership, he's not built for it. A cut, a pier, a reason to be in the same place next year.

He's never committed to anything and he's started to suspect that isn't the same as being free. He's got as far as suspecting it.

recruits.name: Rosa Delgado
recruits.backstory: Eight years guiding in Tanzania taught her that a predator isn't cruel and hunger isn't personal, and she got very tired of explaining both to people who needed the lion to mean something. The savanna didn't care about her. That was most of what she loved about it. Then she got here, where the animals think, where a quilboar runs a plan and changes the plan when it sees you, and she had to stop tracking and start anticipating. She was bad at it for a year. She hadn't been bad at anything in a decade and it nearly took her legs out from under her.
recruits.greeting: Have you got any idea what's living out here? You don't, do you, so yes, I'm coming with you.
recruits.home_note: At the treeline with her kill hung.

background_sections.before: Rosa grew up in a flat in Madrid, about as far from the wild as you can get in Spain. At ten, watching eagles on her grandparents' farm, she decided she was going to Africa, and she did. She spent eight years guiding researchers, photographers and the occasional idiot with money out of Arusha, in Tanzania. Most of the job was sitting absolutely still in the dark. She learned that a predator isn't cruel and hunger isn't personal, and she got very tired of explaining both.
background_sections.adjustment: Here the animals think. A quilboar makes a plan and changes it when it sees you, so she had to stop tracking and start anticipating. She was bad at it for a whole year, and she hadn't been bad at anything in a decade, so it nearly took her legs out from under her. She'll tell anyone straight away that she spent a year being outclassed by pigs. She came out of it a better hunter, and she isn't grateful.
background_sections.now: She works the Central Barrens, which are close enough to savanna to hurt, with dry grass, long sightlines and big animals moving slowly in the heat. She guards the Crossroads road, where the hyenas have worked out what a caravan is. She can tell you what a pack will do four seconds before it does it. She's trying to teach that, and finding it won't go into words.
background_sections.forward: Rosa wants to see the coast, for no particular reason. She grew up a long way from the ocean and spent her career even further from it, and she's decided she's owed. After that she'd like somewhere unmapped. She came for the wild, and the wild keeps turning out to have a road through it.

recruits.name: Marco Rossi
recruits.backstory: Thirty-one years a locksmith in Naples, and for twenty of those the man the neighbourhood sent for when something was wrong and the authorities were worse than the problem. He settled arguments because somebody had to, and because he was the only one everybody owed a favour. The Light found him already doing the work, and he thinks of the whole business as a formality that arrived late.
recruits.greeting: I'll stand right here, ragazzo, and you go and do what you came to do.
recruits.home_note: In the Trade Quarter, keeping the peace by the Seal.

background_sections.before: Marco was a locksmith in Naples for thirty-one years. For twenty of them he was also the man the neighbourhood sent for when something was wrong and the authorities would only make it worse. He settled arguments because somebody had to, and because everybody owed him a favour. He had a wife, Carmela, and two daughters, and a grandson born that February whom he'd held four times.
background_sections.adjustment: He landed in Tirisfal with a half-cut key still in his hand, and he walked to the Undercity because it had doors. Within a fortnight he'd found people to be useful to. Everything else he put off, and he's still putting it off, and at sixty-three he's decided that's a perfectly good way to handle it. The Light found him already doing the work, and he thinks of it as a formality that arrived late.
background_sections.now: He lives in two rooms off the Trade Quarter in the Undercity, where the Forsaken have quietly worked out who to fetch when something's wrong. The Forsaken have a great many locks. He fixes them, and he fixes other things too, and nobody has ever had to ask him. The dead, he says, are much better about paying their debts than the living ever were.
background_sections.forward: Marco wants a neighbourhood again, a few streets where people know to come to him. He's got about half of one in the Undercity now, living and dead. He's counting the passages. He thinks about his grandson every February.

recruits.name: Sophia Dias
recruits.backstory: Fourteen years an interpreter at the European Parliament, simultaneous, in four languages. You hold a sentence in one language while it finishes in another, and you get the tone right as well as the words. Arcane work asks for exactly that kind of attention, held exactly that long. She was better prepared for this than almost anybody, and it took her two years to believe it.
recruits.greeting: Let me think for a moment. You'll get a better answer, and I'll get less shouting.
recruits.home_note: In the Magic Quarter, surrounded by research.

background_sections.before:
A booth, a headset, and a career of being the invisible reason a room understood itself.

She's from Thessaloniki and had been in Brussels for eleven years. Her parents were at home. Greece and Belgium came down on different sides of a mountain range, and she's worked out what that means more carefully than she's admitted to anyone.
background_sections.adjustment:
Two quiet years of being competent and assuming she wasn't.

What broke it was a goblin who asked her to interpret a contract dispute, paid her properly, and then came back.
background_sections.now:
The Undercity, where Forsaken, orcs, trolls, goblins and people from Earth all trade in the same halls in half a dozen languages, and nobody's paid to make that work.

She makes it work, for money, and she's been in the room for three negotiations that would've gone badly without her.
background_sections.forward:
A grammar of this world's arcane. She's convinced magic has a syntax, and that every mage here is speaking it by ear.

She's forty pages in. She's shown it to two people. One of them laughed and the other asked for a copy.

recruits.name: Ryan Murphy
recruits.backstory: Twelve years broking in Boston. Good at it, paid accordingly, and the deals he closed took things from people who never learned his name. He drank after work with men who did the same and agreed with them that it was the system, while not believing it even as he said it, and that's the only real difference between him and them. He expected the frontier to punish him. Instead it handed him a skill that's the same skill: read what a thing wants, work out what it'll take, close. Three years on he's more honest than he's ever been and no better a man, and he'll say so before you can.
recruits.greeting: Everything costs something, and that's not a threat, it's the terms. I'll tell you the price before we start, which is more than my last employer ever did for me.
recruits.home_note: In the Magic Quarter, making deals by the summoning circle.

background_sections.before: Ryan was raised in Cork by his grandmother and spent twelve years as a broker in Boston. He was good at it and paid accordingly, and the deals he closed took things from people who never learned his name. He drank after work with men who did the same and agreed with them that it was just the system, without believing it even as he said it. His son Conor was nineteen and at college in Boston. Ryan is glad, on balance, that his grandmother didn't live long enough to form an opinion of him.
background_sections.adjustment: He expected this world to punish him. Instead it handed him the same skill he'd always had, reading what something wants, working out what it'll take, and closing the deal. He says he hasn't had an adjustment, he's had a diagnosis, and he took it like a man who'd already made it privately. Three years on, he's more honest than he's ever been and no better a man. He'll say so before you can.
background_sections.now: He lives on the Echo Isles, where nobody is under any illusion about anybody, and he finds that restful. His demons are bound by contracts he drafted himself and can recite clause by clause. He pays them on time, exactly on time. That isn't virtue, it's the only thing stopping the arrangement running the other way.
background_sections.forward: Ryan has wanted out of the business for fifteen years without ever taking a step towards it, and he's fluent in all the reasons. Instead he keeps the contracts clean and the terms honest, and tells himself that's different. Conor may well be looking for him somewhere, and Ryan hasn't put his name on a single list in three years. He can give you the reason in one sentence, and he won't.

recruits.name: Carolina Santos
recruits.backstory: Twelve years a river pilot on the Amazon, which means twelve years of reading water that redraws itself every season. A channel that was deep in March will ground you in September. She learned to feel the bottom through the hull. Here the water spirits talk to her, and she describes it as the same conversation she always had with the river, in an accent she had to work at.
recruits.greeting: Everything here has a current, rivers, weather and people. Learn to feel it and you'll stop fighting things that were already carrying you.

background_sections.before: Carolina spent twelve years as a river pilot on the Amazon, guiding cargo boats along a river two kilometres wide that redraws itself every season. A channel that was deep in March can ground you in September. Her grandfather was a pilot before her, and he taught her to feel the riverbed through the hull and to read the colour of the water and the way the birds sat on the banks. She was one of very few women piloting on the river, and the cargo captains trusted her after a single season.
background_sections.adjustment: Her first three years here were gentle, and she knows exactly why. She arrived already believing the water was somebody, so when the water spirits started talking to her, it felt like the same conversation she'd always had with the river, only in a new accent. Half the people from home had to take apart their whole way of seeing the world to cope here. She walked in and recognised the place.
background_sections.now: She lives on the Echo Isles, where the channels between the islands shift with every storm and the Darkspear boatmen lose canoes on the reefs every season. She's been teaching two of them to read the seabed by feel. One of them is starting to get it, and watching that happen has done more for her than three years of being useful. She takes them out in the worst weather on purpose, because that's when the reefs show themselves.
background_sections.forward: Carolina wants a river of her own on this world, a long one with seasons, that she can learn for twenty years and still be surprised by. People keep telling her about a river in Ashenvale, long and wild, that nobody has ever piloted properly. She's heard a great many stories about it. One day she means to find out which of them are true.

recruits.name: Amber Whitehorse
recruits.backstory: Twenty-three years restoring wetland on the Oregon coast. It's a job of doing something slow and correct and having nothing to show anybody for ten years. She planted sedge and waited. She pulled invasive grass for nine years in one basin. Druidry gave her the power to make a thing grow in an afternoon, and the first year she used it constantly, and the second year she mostly stopped.
recruits.greeting: Give it a season. Everything here gives you an answer if you let it finish.
recruits.home_note: Deep in the grove, defending the land.

background_sections.before: Amber grew up in Astoria, on the Oregon coast, where her dad ran a charter boat and her mom taught school. She spent twenty-three years restoring wetland, planting sedge and pulling invasive grass, a job where you do something slow and correct and have nothing to show for it for ten years. She never once got to finish a basin, because the grant money always ran out three years into a thirty-year job. She split from her husband Doug, a forester, in 2016, and lived alone with two dogs after that. She liked it more than she'd expected.
background_sections.adjustment: She was out on the tidal flats in her waders when she found herself in the driest place she'd ever seen. She calls the first eight months the easiest of her life, and she knows that makes her poor company among other people from home. Her whole career had been patience without any power to make things happen. Druidry gave her the power to grow a plant in an afternoon. She used it constantly for a year, and then she mostly stopped.
background_sections.now: She works the oases of the Central Barrens, where a sickness has crept out of the caves and into the water, and the plants are turning into something else. She treats the rot slowly, one oasis at a time, the way she worked her wetlands at home. The tauren and the druids have been watching her for two years. She knows that watching is how they decide whether to trust someone, so she lets them.
background_sections.forward: Amber wants to bring one oasis all the way back, start to finish, the worst one, the one everyone's given up on. After three years here she's further along than twenty-three years of grant cycles ever took her. She's also trying to teach restraint to people who can grow a tree in an afternoon. So far she has one student and a lot of opinions. Her little sister Beth was in Portland, and Amber doesn't let herself think about it too often.

recruits.name: Marcus Okafor
recruits.backstory: He spent a career being right early and watching it change nothing. Models, warnings, briefings to people whose job was deciding the warning was inconvenient. Here the storm answers him. He's been telling everyone he's fine about that since the day it started and everyone believes him, because he's also genuinely fine. Both are true. He's given up trying to reconcile them.
recruits.greeting: The pressure's dropping, listen. That isn't thunder yet, that's the front arriving, and we've got about four minutes before it gets loud and I get useful.

background_sections.before: Marcus was a meteorologist in Toronto. As a student he chased storms, badly and happily, in a battered Corolla. Then he spent fifteen years watching them on screens from somewhere warm, writing warnings and briefing people whose job was deciding the warning was inconvenient. He spent a whole career being right early and watching it change nothing. His mother in Lagos thought the job was a waste of a good degree, and said so every Christmas until the last one.
background_sections.adjustment: He treated the whole thing as fieldwork, and it carried him through almost intact, which is better than most people managed. What wrecked him privately for a year was that at home a storm was something he could predict but never touch. Here the storm answers him. He's told everyone he's fine about that since the day it started, and they believe him, because he really is fine. He's also not, and he's given up trying to make those two things agree.
background_sections.now: He lives in Durotar, where dry storms roll in off the sea with no rain in them and the thunder arrives without warning. His notes on where the lightning strikes have already told him something about this coast that the orcs didn't know. He can't work out how to tell them without sounding like every other outsider who turned up with a clipboard. So far he's kept it in his notebook.
background_sections.forward: Marcus wants a full season's data written up properly, and one person on this world who cares what's in it. He's realistic about the odds, and he keeps the records anyway. What he won't say out loud is that he'd like to stand in the middle of the biggest storm there is. He's a meteorologist, and he knows how that ends.

recruits.name: Ivan Petrov
recruits.backstory: Eleven years a tram driver in Novosibirsk. It's nobody's idea of a story and it's the whole reason he's good at this. Eleven years of a heavy thing on rails with other people's children stepping off the kerb, and he never hit one. He uses a two-handed axe the same way: slow start, committed middle, and knowing exactly how long it takes to stop.
recruits.greeting: Stand where I can see you, please. If you're behind me I'll assume you're the enemy, and I move faster than I apologise.
recruits.home_note: Deep in the chasm, where you found him.

background_sections.before: Ivan drove a tram in Novosibirsk for eleven years, along the same route and past the same four stops in the dark every winter morning. For eleven years he drove a heavy thing on rails while other people's children stepped off the kerb in front of him, and he never hit one. He drove the morning route so he'd be home for dinner with his wife Natasha and their two girls, Sonya and Katya. On Sundays he took the girls skating. He still talks about all three of them in the present tense, every day.
background_sections.adjustment: He expected to be useless here, because he's a tram driver. What he found was that hardly anyone knows how to commit to a movement and then stop it exactly when they mean to. Apparently it's a rare skill. He swings a two-handed axe the way he drove, with a slow start, a committed middle, and a precise sense of how long it takes to stop. He's said more than once that this world has very low standards.
background_sections.now: He lives in Orgrimmar, where the traffic is worse than anything Novosibirsk ever managed and nobody is in charge of it. He's started directing it at the busiest hour, without being asked, and the orcs do what he says. When the cultists in Ragefire Chasm drag somebody off the streets above, he goes down after them. He's usually back in time for dinner.
background_sections.forward: Ivan wants a route again, something fixed, with a timetable. He's asked three different caravan masters whether anybody here runs a regular schedule, and all three laughed at him. He's going to keep asking. He thinks they're the ones being unreasonable, and he may well be right.

recruits.name: Asher
recruits.backstory: Deep South, Bible Belt born and raised, and you can hear it before he says three words. Says the fall into this world felt less like falling and more like being carried, though he laughs it off before it turns into a sermon. He's been camped outside the Coven for two days on his own, alone, waiting on nobody, because somebody's got to and he figures it might as well be him. Doesn't ask why you're here. Just asks if you could use the help, like it's the easiest question in the world.
recruits.greeting: Figure the Good Lord doesn't waste a resurrection on a man who's got nothing left to do with it. There's demons past that ridge. I mean to see to them. Walk with me, if you're willing.
recruits._design_note: Fixed/unchangeable companion - see world/recruit_manager.py RecruitNPC._build_asher_kit for his unique 2-ability kit and hand-authored gear, and /home/claude/frontier_rpg_docs/Asher_Coleman_Character_Profile.docx for the full handoff. Scripted to leave the party permanently after the Baneshadow quest turn-in (see world/quest_manager.py turn_in_quest). No home_town on purpose - he does not offer a find-me-later option at this stage.

background_sections.before:
Deep South, Bible Belt, and you can hear it inside three words. He will tell you about the place and not about himself, and he is so warm about it that you get most of the way home before you notice.

What anyone actually knows: he came through like everybody else, and he says the fall felt less like falling than like being carried. He laughs that off before it turns into a sermon. He always laughs it off.
background_sections.adjustment:
There is no record of Asher having an adjustment, and that is the strangest thing about him.

Everyone else can name their bad year. He was camped outside the Burning Blade Coven within days, alone, waiting for nobody in particular, on the grounds that somebody ought to be and it might as well be him. He asked no questions about where he was. He has still not asked any.
background_sections.now:
Wherever you are. He does not take contracts and he does not go home, and the one time somebody tried to send him back he was simply there the next morning, perfectly friendly about it.

He never asks why you are doing something. He asks if you could use the help, like it is the easiest question in the world, and it is very difficult to say no to.
background_sections.forward:
He has never stated a want. Not once, to anyone, in three years.

Asked, he turns it around and asks about yours, and he is so interested that it works every time. You will not notice he has done it until later, and then you will notice he has done it before.

recruits.name: Owen Pryce
recruits.backstory: Eight years a long-haul driver out of Cardiff, alone in a cab through the small hours, with the radio for company. He talked to himself for a living. Then he got here and something in the dark answered him, and the terrible part is that he was glad. He knows how that sounds. He says it anyway, early, so nobody can say he hid it later.
recruits.greeting: Can you hear that? No, of course you can't, but stay close to me anyway.

background_sections.before: Owen spent eight years as a long-haul lorry driver out of Cardiff, alone in his cab through the small hours with only the radio for company. He talked to himself for a living, and he barely lived in his flat. His mother was in a care home in Barry, and he visited her every second Sunday for six years. By the end she'd forgotten who he was. He says that makes all this easier, and the people who hear him say it understand that it doesn't.
background_sections.adjustment: When something in the dark spoke to him here, the terrible part was that he was glad. He fell straight in, with no moment of resistance, and when he looks at that honestly he finds it worse than the falling. If you press him, he'll say eight years of talking to nobody is good preparation for talking to something. He tells people about it early, so nobody can say he hid it later.
background_sections.now: He works deep in the Azurelode Mine in Western Hillsbrad, where the air is heavy and most people get headaches and leave. Owen hears sentences down there, so he stays. He writes down everything he hears. If he ever goes wrong, he says, somebody will want a record of the route.
background_sections.forward: Owen wants to know what the voice actually wants from him. He's been given hints for three years, and he's tired of hints. He's not sure he'll like the answer. He'd rather know than keep guessing.

recruits.name: Mateo Rojas
recruits.backstory: Seventeen years keeping the lights on at a mountaintop observatory above the Elqui valley. Technician, not astronomer, and he'll correct you on that immediately and then talk for an hour anyway. Up there the sky is so clear it stops being scenery and becomes a place. He arrived on a world with the wrong stars in it and spent his first winter learning them from scratch, alone, on his back in the grass, happier than he'd been in a decade.
recruits.greeting: Look up at it, go on, look up. Three years here and I still have to make people look up.

background_sections.before: Mateo spent seventeen years keeping the lights on at a mountaintop observatory above the Elqui valley in Chile. He was a technician, not an astronomer, and he'll correct you on that immediately and then talk about the stars for an hour anyway. He loved the four hours before dawn, when the astronomers slept and the mountain belonged to him. His wife Paula and their two girls lived in La Serena, and the girls thought the mountain was boring. He agreed with them and went anyway, every month, for seventeen years.
background_sections.adjustment: He arrived on a world with the wrong stars in it and spent his first winter learning them from scratch, alone, lying on his back in the grass. He was happier than he'd been in a decade. The trouble came in his second winter, when he'd finished naming the constellations and had to come back down and be a person again. That took a good deal longer than the stars.
background_sections.now: He lives on top of a mesa in Southern Thousand Needles, where the air is dry and the nights go on forever. The goblins of the Flats think he's harmless and let him climb their towers. From the top of one he can see most of the sky at once. He's started to suspect it's the finest place to watch the stars on this whole world.
background_sections.forward: Mateo is drawing a proper map of this sky, because he understands that a sky is also a calendar, a clock and a promise. He's eleven months into it. Twice a year he walks to Freewind Post with two names folded in his pocket and reads the whole list of the missing. He talks about the stars on the way there and says very little on the way home.

recruits.name: Pasang Lama
recruits.backstory: Nineteen expeditions above eight thousand metres as a climbing guide out of the Solukhumbu. He carried loads for people who went home famous. He's seen what high ground does to a body and to a personality, and he judges strangers by how they behave on day four. The spirits of stone and cold talk to him, and he treats it as a work arrangement rather than a mystery.
recruits.greeting: You need to go slowly. The altitude here is nothing, but your pace is still wrong.

background_sections.before: Pasang guided climbers out of the Solukhumbu, in Nepal, on nineteen expeditions above eight thousand metres. He carried loads for people who went home famous. He's seen what high ground does to a body and to a personality, and he judges strangers by how they behave on day four. Four of his cousins did the same work, and two of them died doing it. He keeps their names to himself.
background_sections.adjustment: He said very little for his first year here. He worked, ate, slept and watched everyone. In his second year he started to speak, and people discovered he'd formed complete opinions about all of them. The spirits of stone and cold talk to him, and he treats it as a working arrangement rather than a mystery.
background_sections.now: He lives high in the Aspen Wilderness, among thin air, golden snow, bad weather and routes nobody ever wrote down. He's written four of them down. He's shown them to one person. The climbers in the Aspen camps ask for him by name, and he turns most of them down after watching them walk.
background_sections.forward: Pasang wants to stand on a summit nobody has ever climbed. The highest peak in the Aspen country has never been reached, and he's heard a great deal of talk from people who've been halfway. He'd like to go alone. He knows that's exactly what he spent nineteen years telling his clients to stop wanting.

recruits.name: Haruto Nakamura
recruits.backstory: Thirty-one years of calligraphy in Kanazawa. The discipline is a single stroke, studied until the hand no longer needs the mind. He trained under a man who corrected him for eleven years before praising him once. Runework here answers to exactly that discipline, and he was the only person who already had it. He calls that luck, and nobody who's watched him work believes him.
recruits.greeting: The form matters, and not for ceremony. A rune cut carelessly fails carelessly, and it fails on whoever's standing closest.

background_sections.before: Haruto practised calligraphy in Kanazawa for thirty-one years, a discipline built on a single stroke studied until the hand no longer needs the mind. He trained under a master who corrected him for eleven years before praising him once. When his master died in 2017, Haruto took over the studio and its four students. He never married, and he'll tell you the work was a full occupation, in a tone that closes the subject.
background_sections.adjustment: Rune magic here answers to exactly the kind of discipline he already had, and he was one of the only people who arrived with it. He calls that luck, and nobody who has watched him work believes him. He simply asked to be taught, and it worked, and he knows almost nobody from home tried that. The old tauren carver who taught him has since died, and Haruto finished the lessons alone, from notes.
background_sections.now: He works in Silverpine South, near the old standing stones, where the dark magic seeping out of the keep has put something into the runes that nobody can read. He's copying them before they fade completely. It's slow work and nobody thanks him for it. His copies will be the only record there is.
background_sections.forward: Haruto thinks four students would be right. He has two, and he won't lower his standards to find another two. He's also putting together a reference of every rune he's ever recorded, in the hope that the discipline will outlast the shortage of teachers. The hope is thin, and he keeps working anyway.

recruits.name: Liam Hartigan
recruits.backstory: Seventeen summers of bushfire season in New South Wales and the bad nights on the highway in between. Firefighter, then paramedic, then both, because the roster never cared which badge you held at three in the morning. The most useful thing in a burning room is a calm voice. The second most useful is a hand on the person about to run. He's good company. He hasn't slept properly since about 2019.
recruits.greeting: I've walked into worse than this, so stay behind me and breathe. I mean it, breathe out loud, where I can hear you doing it.

background_sections.before: Liam spent seventeen summers fighting bushfires in New South Wales, and worked the bad nights on the highway in between. He was a firefighter, then a paramedic, then both, because the roster never cared which badge you held at three in the morning. He learned that the most useful thing in a burning room is a calm voice, and the second most useful is a hand on the person about to run. In 2019 the fires went through the Blue Mountains, and he was on the line for weeks. He went straight back to work afterwards, and that's when he stopped sleeping properly.
background_sections.adjustment: His first year here was the easiest of his life, and his second was the hardest, and he can tell you the exact week it turned. For twelve months there were emergencies everywhere. Then it went quiet for a season, and he found he had no idea what he was for without one. The sun answers him the way a good crew does, when he calls and all at once, and that's most of what holds him together.
background_sections.now: He works the ground around Grom's Rest in Ashenvale East, where the corruption burns out of people slowly and nobody had any procedure for it. He's written one. It's four lines long, wrong in at least one place, and the only one that exists. He's good company, and everybody likes him.
background_sections.forward: Liam wants a crew, properly rostered and trained, that can do the work without him standing there. It's what he wanted at home and never got, because he kept going in alone. There are two children in Grom's Rest whose mother didn't come out of the corruption. He's been in that village for fourteen months, and everyone who knows him can see what's happened except him.

recruits.name: Marta Kowalski
recruits.backstory: Nineteen years of industrial sewing machines in a Łódź plant, which means nineteen years of being the only person in the building who could tell what was wrong from the sound. Management called her whenever a line stopped, and only ever by her first name. Goblin engineering is the same noise with more smoke, and she loves it in a way she'd be embarrassed to have written down.
recruits.greeting: Give it here, please, no, give it here. You've been hitting it, haven't you? People always hit it.

background_sections.before: Marta spent nineteen years looking after the industrial sewing machines at a factory in Lodz, in Poland. She was the only person in the building who could tell what was wrong with a machine from the sound it made, and she could diagnose the whole floor from the doorway. Management called her whenever a line stopped, and only ever by her first name. Her husband Tomasz worked the other shift for fifteen years so that one of them was always home with their boys. They kissed in the doorway twice a day.
background_sections.adjustment: It took her three weeks to settle, and she'll argue that most of that was the language. A machine is a machine, wherever you are. She was repairing goblin gear for money before she could ask where the toilet was. Goblin engineering turned out to be the same noise with more smoke, and she loves it in a way she'd be embarrassed to see written down.
background_sections.now: She works at the Boulder Lode Mine in the Northern Barrens, where everything is broken and the goblins charge a fortune to fix it. She undercuts them by a third and fixes it properly. The goblin foreman has threatened her twice and sent her work three times. Her boys are grown, and Tomasz was on his way to work when it happened.
background_sections.forward: Marta wants her own bench and her own sign, with nobody above her on a floor plan. She's been quoted a price for a corner of the workshop by the pumps, and she can afford it. She's found four reasons to wait. She knows all four are really the same reason.

recruits.name: Callum Reid
recruits.backstory: Sixteen years keeping reptiles at a Queensland sanctuary. Taipans, death adders, and the constant low-grade public relations work of explaining that the animal isn't malicious, it's frightened and you're enormous. He's been envenomated more often than any person should be and files all of it under professional development. His forearms are a map of the learning curve.
recruits.greeting: Don't worry about the scorpion, mate. It's the least dangerous thing on me.

background_sections.before: Callum grew up in Brisbane, where his dad was an electrician and his mum ran a childcare centre, and he spent his childhood catching lizards in the back garden. He went on to keep reptiles at a sanctuary in the Queensland hinterland for sixteen years, looking after taipans, death adders and crocodiles. Most of the job was explaining to school groups that the snake wasn't wicked, it was frightened and they were enormous. He's been bitten more often than any person should be, and he once spent three days in hospital after a taipan nearly killed him.
background_sections.adjustment: He was feeding the animals in the snake house, hook in hand, when the snake house vanished and the Barrens appeared around him. He spent his first eighteen months poisoning himself on purpose, alone, and keeping very poor notes about it. What he got out of it was a working relationship with things that kill people. He says it's the same relationship he had at the sanctuary, only with more interesting animals.
background_sections.now: He lives in the Southern Barrens, within reach of the Wailing Caverns, where the serpents are a great deal more than serpents and don't like visitors. He goes in regularly and comes out reliably. The one time he brought something out alive, the Crossroads made him promise never to do it again, and he promised. He keeps a scorpion on his shoulder and insists she's friendly.
background_sections.forward: Callum wants to go all the way to the bottom of the Wailing Caverns and meet whatever lives down there, and he knows exactly how that sounds. He believes that the animal that bites back is the animal that trusts you, and he'll defend that idea to anyone. He hasn't yet met a creature that wasn't worth the conversation. He misses his blue heeler, Biscuit, more than he misses most people.

recruits.name: Emre Kaya
recruits.backstory: He started at nine, sent to fetch a stuck deadbolt for an uncle in the old bazaar, and found out that every lock is a short conversation with somebody who isn't in the room. Thirty doors a week for most of his life after that. He was never a thief. He was the man you called when you'd locked yourself out of your own livelihood, and he knew the inside of more businesses in that quarter than their owners did. Here the work's identical, except that once, with his picks still in the mechanism, the thing behind the door asked him a question. He got the door open. He's never said whether he answered.
recruits.greeting: A locked door is a conversation, so let me do the talking. Everybody interrupts, and then it takes twice as long.

background_sections.before: Emre started at nine, when an uncle in the old bazaar sent him to deal with a stuck deadbolt. He found out that every lock is a short conversation with someone who isn't in the room, and he opened thirty doors a week for most of his life after that. He was never a thief. He was the man you called when you'd locked yourself out of your own business, and he knew the inside of more shops than their owners did. He watched four old crafts die out in his quarter during his own lifetime.
background_sections.adjustment: He barely had an adjustment worth the name. He found a bigger bazaar with worse customers and had three contented years, which makes him odd company among people from home. He'll admit to someone he likes that part of the reason is that the shop is gone, along with everyone who'd have wanted it run a certain way. He didn't lose a family, he lost an obligation, and he's felt lighter since. He keeps that to himself.
background_sections.now: He's in Eastern Hillsbrad, in the country around Durnholde Keep, a fortress full of doors built by people who took doors seriously. He isn't looting it, he's reading it. He can tell which locks came first and which were added after somebody got in, and so where somebody got in. His mother always said that when one door closes another opens, and he decided around thirty that she meant him.
background_sections.forward: Emre wants to meet the lock that beats him. He hasn't found it yet, and he's started to worry he never will, which is a strange thing to be frightened of. Less romantically, he wants an apprentice, because otherwise the trade dies with him. He's watched that happen to four men he knew, and he doesn't want to be the fifth.

recruits.name: Bakyt Asanov
recruits.backstory: Forty years of high pasture in the Tian Shan, moving a herd up in spring and down in autumn along a route his family has walked for six generations. He reads weather in a sky other people call clear and finds water where there apparently isn't any. The eagle he hunts with here isn't the eagle he hunted with there, and he'll tell you the difference is less than you'd think, and that he grieved the first one properly.
recruits.greeting: Walk behind me and step where I step. The ground lies. It lied at home too, and I've got forty years of practice.

background_sections.before: Bakyt spent forty years on the high pastures of the Tian Shan, in Kyrgyzstan, moving his herd up in spring and down in autumn along a route his family had walked for six generations. His father taught him the route before he could ride, and taught him to hunt with golden eagles. His wife Aigul died of a stroke six years before the Integration, and he kept walking the route alone. Their three sons all went to Bishkek for work. He understood why, and it was still the end of six generations.
background_sections.adjustment: He was bringing the herd up for summer when the herd vanished and he found himself in the hills of Hillsbrad with his eagle glove still on his hand. His old eagle had died the year before, so the glove was empty. He had an easier first year than almost anyone, because nomads adjust, and that's the whole profession. The hard part was quieter. He spent a year of long evenings getting used to the idea that this world has pastures his family will never walk.
background_sections.now: He lives on the high pasture of Eastern Hillsbrad, all grass and wind and long distances between people. The herders out of Tarren Mill move their goats and sheep on a cycle he recognised within a week, and they've started asking his opinion on it. That's the only honour he's ever visibly cared about. He hunts with a new eagle now, called Jeldyz, which means star.
background_sections.forward: Bakyt wants a route of his own, mapped and seasonal and walked often enough that someone else could follow it after him. He has two legs of it so far, and the third crosses high ground where something has been taking the herders' animals. He's fifty-eight, and he's started to think about who will walk it when he can't. The thought has made him friendlier to strangers than he used to be.

recruits.name: Henrik Dahl
recruits.backstory: Twenty-one years a structural engineer in Copenhagen. The discipline is being certain that a thing will hold before anybody stands on it. Arcane magic rewards that temperament more than boldness, which he thinks is the most underappreciated thing about this world. He's precise in conversation to a degree people find either restful or maddening, and he's never managed to predict which.
recruits.greeting: Before we begin, what's the actual objective? I've found that parties rarely agree on it, and they find that out halfway through.

background_sections.before: Henrik was a structural engineer in Copenhagen for twenty-one years, which meant being certain a thing would hold before anyone stood on it. He spent his career doing load calculations and being the person who said no to architects. His wife Mette taught physics at the university. On the morning of the Integration she had a nine o'clock lecture, and it all happened at ten past nine. He's worked out carefully that she'd have been in a lecture theatre, and he stops the calculation right there, every time.
background_sections.adjustment: He spent twenty months treating himself like a structure under an unfamiliar load, testing everything and writing it all down. Arcane magic rewards caution more than boldness, which he thinks is the most underrated thing about this world. His notes are now the most useful record of arcane limits anyone has produced here. He still calls them preliminary, and he'll argue with you if you disagree.
background_sections.now: He works in the Frostward Descent, off Eastern Hillsbrad, as deep into the frozen workings as he can safely go, where magic behaves in ways you can't reproduce anywhere else. He measures everything and has filled eleven notebooks. He'll tell you the eleventh is the only one worth reading. People find his precision either restful or maddening, and he's never managed to predict which.
background_sections.forward: Henrik wants a proper standard, not a spell or a discovery, but a published figure other casters can work to. That way the next person won't have to find the limit with their own body. He's calculated his own limits to four significant figures, and he never goes near them. That's the whole of his method, and it's the reason he's still alive.

recruits.name: Anjali Nair
recruits.backstory: Thirty-one years teaching botany in Pune. Three decades of patience with slow things, and with students who wanted results by Friday. A plant will tell you what it needs if you're willing to wait several seasons for the sentence to finish. Druidry asked her for the same patience and gave her, for the first time in her life, the ability to answer back.
recruits.greeting: Gently, gently, now. Whatever's wrong here, shouting at it will only make it worse, and I've got thirty years of evidence for that.

background_sections.before: Anjali taught botany at a university in Pune for thirty-one years, though her family are Malayali, from Kerala. She grew up in her mother's garden, which was full of plants brought from home. Her students were frightened of her and loved her, and she thought both were correct. Her husband Suresh, an accountant, retired in 2018 and spent two years teaching himself to cook. She had one year of that before his heart gave out, and she calls it the best year of their marriage.
background_sections.adjustment: She was pressing a specimen in the university herbarium, hand lens round her neck, when the herbarium disappeared and Ashenvale was all around her. She took it slowly, which suited her. She treated her whole first year as a field season and kept a notebook the way she'd kept forty of them before. That notebook is now the only careful record of Ashenvale's undergrowth in any language, and she still thinks of it as a draft.
background_sections.now: She works in Ashenvale West, where the forest is sick in a pattern that the night elves feel in their bones but have never written down. Anjali is writing it down. The Sentinels were suspicious of her for two years, and now they bring her specimens. She'll tell you the Latin name of anything you pass, whether you've asked or not.
background_sections.forward: Anjali wants to be read in two hundred years, and she says it cheerfully and means every word. That means a copy of her notebook kept somewhere safe, in a language that will last, and a student who cares about it as much as she does. She has the notebook, and she's working on the rest. Her son Arjun and his daughter Meera were in Bangalore, and she presses a leaf for Meera every week.

recruits.name: Hana Tamihana
recruits.backstory: Fourteen summers of black sand and heavy water on the Waikato coast, and a rip that took somebody every few years no matter how many signs went up. She's pulled a lot of people out. She remembers the two she didn't, by name, including the one whose family still won't speak to her. She was nineteen when she got here, into a world of people with whole careers behind them, and she spent a year being treated as the kid. That's the part that actually stung.
recruits.greeting: Stay on my left and don't argue with the water. It's not your mate and it's not your enemy, it's just honest. People drown because they try to bargain with it.

background_sections.before: Hana spent fourteen summers as a lifeguard on a black sand beach on the Waikato coast of New Zealand, where a rip took somebody every few years no matter how many signs went up. Her uncle Rawiri sat in the same tower before her. She pulled a lot of people out of that water, and she remembers the two she couldn't, by name. That year she was finally going to university to study marine science, after deferring twice because she couldn't bear to leave the beach.
background_sections.adjustment: Her whole family was at the beach that Sunday morning for her cousin's birthday, and she was up in the tower when everything changed. She had less to unlearn than most people, and she'll tell you that's luck, not merit. The tide spirits read her the way she reads a wave, and she understood them within a week. Her real struggle was being nineteen in a world full of people with whole careers behind them, and being treated as the kid for a year.
background_sections.now: She works the Hillsbrad coast now, which is colder and greyer than home but has the same undertow. She's been teaching the fishing families to read it, and two of them listen. One of those two has stopped losing nets. That's done more for her standing on the coast than anything she could have said about herself.
background_sections.forward: Hana wants a bigger sea, and she says it lightly and means it. There's a coast on the far side of Ashenvale where people say the water does something nobody can describe properly, and she's determined to see it. Astranaar is on the way, and that's where the big lists of the missing go up. Her family is somewhere, and at twenty-two she isn't ready to accept somewhere the way older people have.

recruits.name: Kesten Ambrose
recruits.backstory: Tallinn, the city archive, twenty-six years among acid-free boxes. Then a serial number in a Scourge ledger. Then neither. What came back has the archivist's habits and little of his warmth, and he is the first to say so. He catalogues. It is the only continuity he has and he defends it the way other people defend a family.
recruits.greeting: Kesten. Formerly a serial number. I have selected the name and I would ask you to use it.

background_sections.before: Kesten spent twenty-six years at the city archive in Tallinn, among acid-free boxes, quietly convinced that a thing nobody recorded had never quite happened. He was a warm man then, by all accounts, though he can no longer vouch for it himself. He had a wife. He keeps her name written down now, because he doesn't trust himself to hold onto it, and he says the written record is enough. Nobody who hears him say that thinks it's enough at all.
background_sections.adjustment: He didn't adjust to this world in the usual way, because he died in it. The Scourge took him and wrote him down in a ledger as a serial number, and later he came back, partly, as something that has the archivist's habits and little of his warmth. He's been taking an inventory of what returned ever since. That inventory is the document he values most, and he won't show it to anyone.
background_sections.now: He lives at Kael's Bastion now, and he travels back to Tirisfal, near the ground where he was processed, where the Scourge's ledgers are still legible if you know the handwriting. He knows the handwriting. He's been reading his own entry for two years and has never told anyone what it says. He chose the name Kesten himself, and he'd like you to use it.
background_sections.forward: Kesten means to write a complete record of how the Scourge worked, by something that was inside it. He knows what he's for now, and he's decided to be for that on purpose rather than by default. He doesn't expect to finish. The expectation has never once slowed him down.

recruits.name: Tarek Mansour
recruits.backstory: Fourteen years a civil engineer in Cairo. Water systems: pressure, pumps, the unglamorous arithmetic of a city that drinks. He was good at it and he was careful about everything else, for a long time, until a colleague made a telephone call about him and the wrong office took an interest. He left in a week with two bags and an engineering degree nobody in Berlin would look at. The faith he carries now is not the one that was used against him, and he will sit with you for an hour explaining the difference to anyone prepared to be serious about it.
recruits.greeting: Tell me plainly where I'm needed and I'll be there. I've had my fill of the other kind of instruction, from people who were very sure they were doing right.

background_sections.before: Tarek spent fourteen years as a civil engineer in Cairo, designing the pipes and pumps that kept a city of twenty million in water. He lived in a small flat in Heliopolis that he could still draw from memory if he let himself. For six of those years he was with a man called Omar, who taught chemistry at a secondary school and laughed at everything, including the danger they were in. They were careful for a long time, until one evening at a wedding they weren't, and someone made a phone call. Tarek left the country within a week, and Omar stayed behind with his parents and his sister.
background_sections.adjustment: Tarek is one of the few people who'll tell you plainly that this world has been better to him than the last one, and it tends to quiet a room. He gives two reasons, and always in the same order. The first is that whatever is poisoning the water here is an enemy he can see and fight, and he spent twenty years wishing for something that simple. The second he says more quietly. In three years here, nobody has asked him a question he had to lie about.
background_sections.now: He works the streams of Ashenvale East, where the water carries the corruption further than the corruption can walk. He's mapped which springs are still clean and which only look it, and the Splintertree garrison now sends for him before it sends for a priest. The orcs have offered him a title twice, and he's turned it down both times without giving a reason. The reason is that he's seen what happens when one man gets to decide who belongs.
background_sections.forward: What he wants is a well that's still standing in ten years. He's sunk three so far, and one has already failed, and he'll happily explain why with a stick in the dirt. He doesn't call it rebuilding any more. He calls it building, because nothing here was ever his to rebuild. Every few months he walks down to Astranaar to read the Cairo lists, and Omar has never been on them, which he knows tells him very little.

recruits.look: Egyptian man in his late 30s, medium height and thickening at the middle, close-cropped black hair receding at the temples, heavy brows, a careful unhurried face. Dark leather tank harness over a padded gambeson in sand and oxblood, a broad round shield, a short heavy blade kept sheathed. A pair of white cotton conservator's gloves folded through his belt, laundered grey.

recruits.name: Fiona Strachan
recruits.backstory: Nine years investigating fraud for an energy company, on North Sea rigs and out of its Dublin office. The whole trade is noticing the one entry that doesn't fit and then being unbearable about it until somebody checks. She was very unpopular and quite often right. The thing that hunts people here leaves a trail of the same shape as a cooked ledger: too neat, and neat in the places nobody looks.
recruits.greeting: I've read your file, and not literally, before you ask. I'm telling you it's a habit of mine, and you'll want to know about it before we work together.

background_sections.before: Fiona spent nine years investigating fraud for an energy company, flying out to North Sea rigs and working out of the Dublin office. The whole job was spotting the one entry that didn't fit and then being unbearable about it until somebody checked. She was very unpopular and quite often right. She once shut down a rig her own brother Graeme worked on, over a falsified safety record. Half the crew never forgave her, and Graeme did, eventually.
background_sections.adjustment: She treated her first year here as a filing exercise, cataloguing every corrupted thing she came across in a notebook that's now more useful than she is. Some time in her second year she realised she'd been treating a war like a backlog of cases. That landed hard. She still files everything, but now she knows why she does it.
background_sections.now: She works out of a rented room in Booty Bay full of files. People are being taken from the coastal villages of Southern Stranglethorn by a cult in the jungle, and nobody had mapped the pattern until she started. She has three hundred pages now, all cross-referenced. She carries the whole thing on her back, because she won't leave a copy anywhere she can't see it.
background_sections.forward: Fiona wants to finish her catalogue and hand it to someone who'll actually act on it. Both halves matter, and the second is the one she keeps failing at. She's had the same conversation with the Booty Bay authorities four times now. She took minutes of all four.

recruits.look: Scottish woman in her mid 40s, tall and square-built, sandy-grey hair cut short and shoved back, weather-ruined face, pale eyes set deep. Blackened mail over a long coat in slate and rust, a heavy tower shield slung at her back, a flanged mace at her hip. A yellow offshore survival-suit whistle still clipped to her collar on a fraying lanyard.

recruits.name: Pavlo Hryn
recruits.backstory: Sixteen years a Lviv schoolteacher, history, fourteen-year-olds. The work is standing in front of a room that would rather be anywhere else and keeping it together by presence alone. He does the same thing in a shield wall and finds it considerably easier, because a gnoll at least wants something comprehensible.
recruits.greeting: Give me the line and I'll hold it. Tell me how long for, though, because I'd rather know.

background_sections.before: Pavlo taught history to fourteen-year-olds at a school in Lviv for sixteen years. The job was standing in front of a room that would rather be anywhere else and holding it together through presence alone. He disagreed with the curriculum and taught it anyway, and he reached most of his thirty students a year. Every spring he taught the same four wars. He thought it was the most important job in the world.
background_sections.adjustment: He'll tell you openly that it went badly. For a whole year he looked for a school, and there wasn't one. What there was, was plenty of work for a man who'd stand still while something came at him, so he took it. Taking it was a small grief, and he's never dressed it up as a calling. It's taken him most of three years to stop feeling wounded that nobody here needs a history teacher.
background_sections.now: He's at the Sepulcher in Silverpine North, holding the road against whatever comes up it from the south. He finds a shield wall much easier than a classroom, because a gnoll at least wants something he can understand. It's steady work and he's good at it. He'd swap it tomorrow.
background_sections.forward: Pavlo is teaching again, six children at the Sepulcher twice a week, whatever he can remember of a world that isn't coming back. He's not sure it's useful, and he does it anyway. Two of the children have stopped coming. He's decided not to ask why.

recruits.look: Ukrainian man in his early 50s, huge through the shoulders and gone soft over it, shaved head, grey stubble, a nose broken long ago and badly set. Dark iron plate with a black tabard and a greatshield, faint ember-red light in the seams of the gauntlets. A steel thermos flask, dented and lidless, strapped where a water flask should go.

recruits.name: Jun-seo Park
recruits.backstory: Nine years on a Busan line, night shift mostly, the same two motions ten thousand times a day. His body learned things his mind never had a say in. Here that's a weapon: he moves without deciding to and it's fast, and the only thing that frightens him about it is how little of it he chooses.
recruits.greeting: I stood in the same two square metres for twelve hours a day, nine years running. Whatever this turns out to be, it'll be easier than that.

background_sections.before: Jun-seo worked on a factory line in Busan for nine years, mostly night shifts, making the same two motions ten thousand times a day. He could draw his two square metres of floor from memory. Every month for nine years he sent money home to his parents. His body learned things on that line that his mind never had any say in.
background_sections.adjustment: In his first year here he worked, at anything, for anyone, as many hours as there were. In his second year somebody finally made him sit down, and he discovered he had no idea what to do with a free day. He'll tell you that was a worse problem than anything in the first year. His body still moves without him deciding to, and in a fight it's very fast. What frightens him is how little of it he chooses.
background_sections.now: He runs the cargo hoist at a goblin camp in Central Stranglethorn, hauling crates up from the river. It's two motions, ten thousand times a day, and he's well aware of the joke. He keeps the job anyway. In the evenings he carves wood, very slowly and very badly.
background_sections.forward: Jun-seo wants to be slow at something, not good at it, just slow. He picked woodcarving because it can't be hurried, and he's catastrophically bad at it, which is the point. He's tried to explain this twice, and neither person understood. He doesn't talk about whether his parents are alive, because he isn't ready to.

recruits.look: South Korean man in his early 40s, wiry and slightly stooped, black hair shot with grey and flattened by a helmet, a long patient face, deep smile lines he does not use often. Grey-black mail with a hooded mantle and a scythe-headed polearm carried butt-down. A welder's flip-up shade, cracked across one lens, pushed up on his forehead.

recruits.name: Minh Tran
recruits.backstory: Twenty-three years of air traffic control at Tân Sơn Nhất. The job is holding forty futures in your head at once and choosing the one where nobody dies. Time magic asked him for exactly that, and nothing he hadn't already done for twenty years on three hours' sleep. He's the calmest person in most rooms, and it's professional conditioning, not temperament.
recruits.greeting: One moment, please. I'd like to work out the sequence of events before we add anything to it.

background_sections.before: Minh spent twenty-three years in air traffic control at Tan Son Nhat airport in Ho Chi Minh City. The job meant holding forty possible futures in his head at once and choosing the one where nobody died. He learned never to let his voice show what his pulse was doing. His daughter Linh was studying music in Melbourne, and he's allowed himself to believe the hopeful version of where she is.
background_sections.adjustment: He was on shift, in the middle of handing over to the next controller, when everything changed. He says the handover was the hardest part, and people assume he means the Integration. He means the handover. He'd just said the words you have control, and then he was gone, and he'll never know what happened to those forty aircraft.
background_sections.now: He keeps watch from a stone hut on a ridge in the Northern Barrens, above a dry riverbed where time slips. Now and then water from years ago runs through it for an hour, or a caravan arrives before it set out. Almost nobody understands how dangerous that is, so he's appointed himself to watch it. He's made a rota of one.
background_sections.forward: Minh would like one hour in which nothing at all is his responsibility. He hasn't had one since 2003, and he's beginning to suspect the problem isn't the schedule. In the meantime he keeps watching the riverbed, because nobody else will. He knows that's exactly the reasoning that got him here.

recruits.look: Vietnamese man in his late 30s, slight and neat, black hair parted and kept flat, round wire glasses, an attentive head-tilted way of standing. Pale blue and bone-white robes with long cuffs and a brass-ringed orrery at the belt, a slim staff with a slow-turning ring at its head. A tuning fork on a cord round his neck, the tines worn bright.

recruits.name: Alonso Vega
recruits.backstory: Twenty-two years running the kiln at his family's Talavera workshop in Puebla. Glaze, temperature, timing: a trade where the whole year's work turns on four hours of heat going exactly right. He feels a fire the way other people feel a draught. Here fire answers him, and the first thing he did with that was make a cup, badly, and he keeps it on a shelf.
recruits.greeting: Give me room when I work, and then give me a bit more than that. I've burnt three people's eyebrows off being polite about it.

background_sections.before: Alonso ran the kiln at his family's Talavera pottery workshop in Puebla for twenty-two years, the same kiln his grandfather had fired for forty years before him. A whole year's work turned on four hours of heat going exactly right, and he learned to feel a fire the way other people feel a draught. His wife Lupe sold their blue and white pottery at the market, and she could sell anything to anybody. Their two sons, Rodrigo and Fernando, moved to Mexico City, and neither of them wanted the kiln. He minded more than he ever said.
background_sections.adjustment: He was four hours into a firing, with his kiln goggles round his neck, when he found himself standing in the jungle. It took him about ten weeks to settle, and he treated this world like a new kiln with a strange character, learning it the way he'd learned four others. Fire answered him here, and the first thing he did with it was make a cup, badly. Lupe was at the market when it happened. He's said the word market perhaps twice in three years, and changed the subject both times.
background_sections.now: He lives among the jungle ruins of Central Stranglethorn, beside an old troll fire-pit where they once fired their idols. It's the hottest place he's found, so it's the only place he wants to be. He keeps a pot going in a crack in the rock that nobody is supposed to know about. The bad cup he made in his first week sits on a shelf beside it, and he won't let anyone move it.
background_sections.forward: Alonso wants a kiln of his own, built properly, with someone to teach. He's found the clay and he's found the site, and he's been putting it off for two years. The reason he gives is money, but the reason isn't money. Building it would mean admitting he's staying, and admitting he's staying means thinking about the market.

recruits.look: Mexican man in his mid 40s, broad and short, thick black hair pushed back off a high forehead, forearms shiny with old burn scars, a wide easy face. Deep orange and ash-grey robes cut short at the sleeve for the heat, a censer-headed staff trailing warm light. A pair of smoked-glass glassblower's goggles hung at his throat.

recruits.name: Delroy Beckford
recruits.backstory: Thirty-one years of nights in a bakery on Spanish Town Road. In at eleven, out at seven, measuring by hand and by feel. He knew the weather by how the dough behaved and the regulars by what they bought. A brew is a dough with different patience. He treats a wounded party like an order going out at dawn: everybody gets something, nobody waits long, and the complaining is part of the process.
recruits.greeting: Sit down and drink that, and no, I'm not telling you what's in it. I fed a whole city its breakfast for thirty-one years, and not one of them ever asked what was in the bread.

background_sections.before: Delroy spent thirty-one years working nights at a bakery on Spanish Town Road in Kingston. He went in at eleven at night and came out at seven in the morning, measuring everything by hand and by feel. He knew the weather by how the dough behaved and knew his regulars by what they bought. His wife Marcia died when he was forty-six, and he kept working nights, because the nights were when he missed her least. He's never been awake at the same hours as everyone else, and he's never called it a sacrifice.
background_sections.adjustment: It was four in the morning by his clock when everything changed, and he likes to say that's the only reason he wasn't asleep for it. It's mostly a joke. He found out quickly that a brew is just a dough with a different kind of patience. He treats a wounded party the way he treated the morning orders, where everybody gets something, nobody waits long, and the complaining is part of the process.
background_sections.now: He works out of the lower gallery in Booty Bay, where the work on the piers breaks people steadily and the Baron doesn't care. He still works nights out of habit, and the dockhands have formed a queue for him that pretends not to be a queue. Every ship that ties up gets asked about the same three names. The Bay thinks it's a sweet habit of the old baker's, but it's a system, and in three years it's turned up one maybe.
background_sections.forward: Delroy wants an oven first, and then an apprentice, in that order, and he won't be hurried on either. He's been offered a share in a Booty Bay kitchen twice, and he's turned it down both times. He gives his reasons freely, and nobody finds them convincing. The truth is that he wants to bake bread again, and he wants it to be his.

recruits.look: Jamaican man in his early 50s, tall and lean with a slight permanent stoop, grey locs tied back, a long lined face that goes from grave to delighted with no warning. Leather and woven-grass healer's gear in moss and bone, a cauldron-bowl slung at the hip and a short paddle-like stave. A floury canvas apron, folded and tied at the waist, never quite clean.

recruits.name: Imelda Salonga
recruits.backstory: Fish on a Navotas quay from five in the morning, boxing in the evenings, the same six streets her whole life. Ten fights a year, and she won more than she lost. Her healing isn't gentle and doesn't look like healing. She hits things and her people get better. Freewind Post took about a week to stop asking and most of a year to stop watching her sideways while it worked.
recruits.greeting: I know how it looks, so just stay behind me and watch. When I land one, you'll feel it, and don't ask me to explain, because I couldn't explain it in my own language either.

background_sections.before: Imelda sold fish on a quay in Navotas, near Manila, from five every morning, and boxed every evening at a gym above a tyre shop. She lived her whole life within the same six streets. She fought about ten times a year and won more than she lost, and she always wrapped her own hands, because nobody else did it tight enough. Her mother called the boxing a phase for nineteen years.
background_sections.adjustment: She arrived at market hour with her hands already wrapped, and she calls that luck. Her healing turned out to be anything but gentle. She hits things, and her people get better, and it doesn't look like healing at all. Freewind Post took about a week to stop asking what she was doing, and most of a year to stop watching her sideways while she did it.
background_sections.now: She works at Freewind Post, where the tauren ride the lifts and the drop does the rest, and the injured come in steadily all week. The Post asks for her by name without being able to say what she is. Two summers ago her mother turned up on a goblin barge, having asked after her in four languages all the way down the coast. Her mother lives at the Post now, and she still calls the boxing a phase.
background_sections.forward: Imelda has been asking around the arena whether anybody here fights properly, with rules, a count and somebody keeping time. Every answer has been enthusiastic, and none of them has been about that. She's getting tired of explaining the difference. She still wraps her hands every morning before anything else, breakfast included.

recruits.look: Filipina woman in her mid 30s, compact and visibly strong through the shoulders, black hair in a short practical knot, flat nose, a scar through one eyebrow. Mail and green hide cut for movement, wrapped fists, no shield and no staff at all. A pair of soft hand-wraps from a boxing gym, washed to grey, rewound every morning.

recruits.name: Tomas Havel
recruits.backstory: Eighteen years up in the grid in Prague, on tour and in theatres, at four in the morning, hanging weight over the heads of people who'd never look up. The job was leverage, timing, and never being the reason something fell. He swings a two-hander like a man who's spent his life moving heavy things through small gaps.
recruits.greeting: Big sword, lots of room. Tell me where you want me standing before it starts, not during. I've worked with people who shout during, and I didn't enjoy any of them.

background_sections.before:
A bad shoulder from a truss in 2014 that he worked through because the show was that night. It still tells him when the weather's turning, and he still works through it.

There was a woman in Prague, Klára, he hadn't asked yet, and before her a lighting tech called Dominik who asked him first and had a yes inside the week. The crew ran a book on which way he'd go. He refused to settle it, mostly because he liked watching the money change hands.
background_sections.adjustment:
He arrived forty feet up, in the air over Fenris Isle, and landed in a tree. That should have killed him, and he can't tell the story without it coming out as a brag. He's given up fixing the delivery and gets it over with early.

Three years is long enough that he's started talking about Dominik and Klára in the past tense without noticing. His friends here have noticed.
background_sections.now:
Fenris Isle and whatever scaffolding he can reach, because people here build fast and tie off badly and he physically can't walk past it.

He's paid in food and the occasional argument.
background_sections.forward:
Something that stays up.

He's been looking at the way people here hold their roofs on with an expression they find difficult to read, and they've decided not to ask about it.

recruits.look: Czech man in his early 40s, rangy and long-armed, dark hair cut short, a thin face with a permanent squint from years of looking up into lights. Battered plate with the pauldrons stripped off for reach, a two-handed sword worn across the back. A steel carabiner clipped to his belt loop, scratched to bare metal.

recruits.name: Eino Virtanen
recruits.backstory: Twenty-six years felling timber in Lapland. Six months of dark a year, machinery, and nobody to talk to for days at a stretch. The axe is the same axe. He talks about as much as the work requires. People read that as unfriendliness for the first month and then stop.
recruits.greeting: The cold doesn't bother me, so go on, say something about the sauna. Everybody does, and I've stopped minding.
