background_sections.before: Eino felled timber in Lapland for twenty-six years, through six months of darkness every year, often with nobody to talk to for days at a time. His family had cut and replanted the same stretch of forest, about the size of a county, for four generations. His brother Juha sold his half to a company that clear-cut it in a single winter. The two of them haven't spoken since. Eino still thinks about the trees that came down that year.
background_sections.adjustment: He says there was nothing to his adjustment, because the trees here are just bigger. The axe is the same axe, and the work is the same work. The heat is the only thing he's never got used to. He built himself a sauna anyway, in the middle of the jungle, and everyone thinks he's lost his mind.
background_sections.now: He works at a goblin logging camp in Northern Stranglethorn, cutting jungle trees the size of towers, and he lives in the only hut there with a sauna. The goblin crews hire him by the season and have given up trying to make conversation. He prefers it that way, and he thinks they do too. People take his silence for unfriendliness for about a month, and then they stop noticing it.
background_sections.forward: Eino wants to see the cold north of this world one day, for reasons he can't explain. People have told him it's worse than Lapland, and that hasn't put him off at all. In the meantime he plants a tree for every one he cuts, quietly, at night. He's never told anyone why, but it's because of Juha.

recruits.look: Finnish man in his late 30s, enormous and pale, red-blond hair and a thick beard, small light eyes, a face that gives away nothing. Heavy hide and fur over bare arms, a hand axe in each fist. A length of orange pipeline marking tape knotted round one bicep, faded to salmon.

recruits.name: Ziad Haddad
recruits.backstory: Six years a paramedic in Beirut, a city that taught him triage as a reflex and the bitter arithmetic of a van with four spaces. He made those choices for six years, and every one was correct, and every one cost him something. Fel magic put a terrible, obvious power in reach, and he took it, for the same reason he chose the fourth patient over the fifth.
recruits.greeting: Keep moving, I'm serious. Everything bad that happened to me happened while I was standing still.

background_sections.before:
A van, a radio, and a city where the road you took mattered more than the medicine you carried.

His parents and his little sister Lina are in Beirut, or were. He doesn't let himself look very hard.
background_sections.adjustment:
Twelve months of saying yes to things he should have slept on.

He owns all of it. What he refuses is the suggestion that it was weakness. He was offered the ability to save more people and he took it, and three years on he's still doing the arithmetic in public, out loud, for anyone who wants to argue.
background_sections.now:
The country around Booty Bay in Southern Stranglethorn, where the Bloodsail, the trolls and the jungle trade blows with the town and the casualties are constant.

He's first on scene, always. The jungle trolls have a word for him, and he's asked three times what it means and got three different answers.
background_sections.forward:
Out of the fel, for good. He's looked into what getting out of the fel costs, and the figure is the reason he's still in.

In the meantime he works. The people he pulls out are alive either way, and that's his whole defence, and he knows how thin it is.

recruits.look: Lebanese man in his early 30s, slim and quick, black curls kept long on top, a sharp handsome face he is aware of, dark eyes with a faint green cast now. Purple-black leathers cut close with a half-cape, twin curved blades, a thin fel shimmer on the edges. A single foam earplug on a cord, tucked behind his collar.

recruits.name: Pieter Malan
recruits.backstory: Twenty-eight years in Rotterdam port safety. Harnesses, exclusion zones, and the deeply unglamorous business of nobody dying today. He's been shouted at by thousands of men in a hurry and outlasted all of them. He stands in front of a party now and runs the same arithmetic he always has. A precaution costs less than the thing it prevents, every time, on any world.
recruits.greeting: I'll take the hits, and that isn't courage, it's arithmetic. I'm the one wearing the armour.

background_sections.before: Pieter spent twenty-eight years in port safety at Rotterdam, dealing with harnesses, exclusion zones and the deeply unglamorous business of nobody dying today. He carried a clipboard and a hard hat and had a reputation as the most tedious man on the docks. He was shouted at by thousands of men in a hurry and outlasted every one of them. He believed a precaution always costs less than the thing it prevents.
background_sections.adjustment: He settled in instantly, and he's slightly ashamed of how fast it was. His entire profession turned out to apply directly to a world full of monsters. His old colleagues in Rotterdam would have found that hilarious. He stands at the front of a party now and runs the same arithmetic he always has.
background_sections.now: He works at the goblin dig sites of Northern Tanaris, where men and goblins work deep pits and high scaffolds without harnesses, and the Cartel's position is that they chose the job. Pieter has pulled nine men out of trouble in three years. He keeps count, because somebody should. The goblins call him the Nuisance, and they mean it fondly.
background_sections.forward: Pieter wants rules that will outlive him. He's written a full set for the dig sites, and the Cartel foreman has ignored every one. He submits them again every season, and he's done it four seasons running. He'll keep going until somebody signs.

recruits.look: South African man in his mid 40s, heavy and sunburnt, thinning blond hair, a flat pugnacious face, forearms like a man who has swung things for a living. Dull gold plate worn open at the throat, a one-handed mace and a shield he uses offensively. A groundsman's folding knife on a belt loop, handle worn pale.

recruits.name: Esteban Ruiz
recruits.backstory: Nineteen years a surgeon in Valparaíso. The work is doing a violent thing for a good reason, with absolute precision, while the person on the table trusts you entirely. Blood magic is the same thing with the formalities removed. He finds the honesty of it a relief and the company it attracts a continual disappointment.
recruits.greeting: There's a price, and I'll name it before we go any further. I'd ask you not to pretend afterwards that I didn't.

background_sections.before: Esteban was a surgeon in Valparaiso for nineteen years. He describes surgery as doing a violent thing for a good reason, with absolute precision, while the person on the table trusts you completely. He insisted on explaining every consent form properly, even when nobody wanted him to. He was respected and not much liked. He didn't mind either way.
background_sections.adjustment: He didn't have a crisis when he arrived, he took an inventory. Within the first month he'd confirmed that his skill had come with him whole. Blood magic turned out to be surgery without the formalities, and he found the honesty of it a relief. What he hadn't expected was how much of his restraint had come from the hospital rather than from himself. He found that out in his second year, on a Bloodsail ship, and he didn't enjoy it.
background_sections.now: He works in Orgrimmar now, in a room near the healers, and the orc and troll healers have started letting him work alongside them. He treats anyone who comes to him. He asks how they got hurt every time, and writes it down, and then he treats them anyway. The kind of people blood magic attracts are a constant disappointment to him.
background_sections.forward: Esteban wants a written standard of practice that binds anyone who claims to use blood magic. Nothing like it exists on this world, and that appals him. He's drafted eleven rules so far. He doesn't expect anyone to adopt them, and he keeps drafting.

recruits.look: Argentinian man in his late 30s, medium build and going grey early at the front, neat beard, an unsettlingly calm bedside manner. Dark red leathers with a lamellar chest and a thin crimson blade, faint red light under the skin of his forearms. A radiation-badge dosimeter clipped at his collar, the window long since gone black.

recruits.name: Kiet Somsak
recruits.backstory: Eleven years a motorcycle courier in Bangkok, which means eleven years of being invisible in traffic and arriving before anyone expected. He went into offices, kitchens and back rooms all day long, and nobody ever looked at him twice. He kept a great deal of what he overheard. Here the skill transfers whole, and he's been careful to let very few people work out that it's a skill.
recruits.greeting: Keep your voice down. Half of what I know, I learned from people who thought nobody was listening.

background_sections.before: Kiet spent eleven years as a motorcycle courier in Bangkok, weaving through traffic in a city where the fastest route changed every hour. He walked into offices, kitchens and back rooms all day long, and nobody ever looked at him twice, so he heard a great deal. He lived with his grandmother, Yai Boonsri, in Khlong Toei. She was eighty-four and couldn't manage the stairs, so he carried her up and down every day, and she called him her legs.
background_sections.adjustment: It took him six weeks to settle, and he had a route across the Tanaris desert before he had a bed. He says the hard part was the quiet. After eleven years of engine noise, he'd landed in a world where he could hear people breathing two rooms away. Three years on, he still flinches at silence, and that's going more slowly than everything else.
background_sections.now: He works the Abyssal Sands, south of Tanaris, carrying things between the camps faster than anyone else can. People talk freely around the person carrying something, and nobody watches him. He's mapped the whole desert by how long each route takes at each hour of the day. It's the first thing he does anywhere, and he's stopped being surprised that nobody else does it.
background_sections.forward: Kiet wants a standing arrangement with somebody who'll pay for information and ask for it politely. He's had three offers so far, and all three came from people he'd rather owe nothing to. He's careful to let very few people work out that listening is a skill. He thinks about his grandmother every time he climbs a flight of stairs.

recruits.look: Thai man in his late 20s, small and economical in his movements, black hair cut short, a quiet watchful face, hands that are never still. Matte grey-green leathers with a soft hood down, a thin dagger at the small of the back. A brass key blank on a loop of wire at his belt, cut for nothing.

recruits.name: Stelios Dukas
recruits.backstory: Nineteen years a funeral director in Thessaloniki. The trade is composure, paperwork, and being the steadiest person in the worst room of somebody's life. He's unshockable in a way that has nothing to do with callousness, and his profession prepared him for this world considerably better than anybody's did who arrived with a weapon.
recruits.greeting: I handled the dead for nineteen years before any of this. The difference now is that they occasionally have something to add.

background_sections.before:
Arrangements, families, and the particular courtesy of a man who's told four thousand people the worst thing they'll hear that year.

The business was his father's. He's said that inheriting it wasn't a choice, and that he'd have chosen it, and that both of those are true, and that people find the combination difficult.
background_sections.adjustment: He was calm throughout, and he's tired of being praised for it. Composure was his job for nineteen years. You might as well praise a baker for being awake.
background_sections.now:
Glittervein, past the Abyssal Sands, where there are many dead and nobody else to keep records of them.

He does the paperwork. He's extremely good at it, and he's used it four times now to find out who a body was before it stopped being anyone.
background_sections.forward:
Rites, proper ones, for the people from Earth who die here with nobody who knows their language.

He's conducted one hundred and forty. He keeps a register, and he's written to every hub he can reach asking that the names be posted, and three have replied.

recruits.look: Greek man in his early 50s, tall and gaunt, grey hair worn too long, a dry ironic face, half-moon reading glasses on a chain. Charcoal and bone robes with a high collar, a staff topped with a bound sheaf of pages. A librarian's date stamp, brass and wooden-handled, carried in a robe pocket.

recruits.name: Ratih Pranoto
recruits.backstory: Fifteen years a forest ranger in Sumatra, which meant long patrols, poachers, and a government that funded the uniforms and little else. She learned to read a forest for the one wrong thing in it: a snare, a path, a silence where there should be birds. Out on the salt the method is the same, and it's easier to see the wrong thing where nothing hides.
recruits.greeting: You need to walk quieter. I can hear you from the other end of the valley, and so can everything else.

background_sections.before: Ratih spent fifteen years as a forest ranger in Sumatra, walking long patrols, chasing poachers and working for a government that paid for the uniforms and little else. She learned to read a forest for the one wrong thing in it, a snare, a path, a silence where there should be birds. She was often the only person in the province who seemed to care. Her sister Dewi lived in Medan with her son Arif, and Ratih had promised to visit that summer, after one more patrol.
background_sections.adjustment: She went straight to work. Within a month she'd invented a patrol route of her own, without anyone's permission. Her second year was harder, for a reason she finds absurd. Out here, people thank her, and she still doesn't know what to do with it.
background_sections.now: She walks the Shimmering Flats on a route she drew herself, looking for the one wrong thing, a trap, a hidden cache, a track that shouldn't be there. Out on the salt it's easier to spot, because nothing can hide. She reports every find to the tauren at Freewind Post. She signs none of the reports.
background_sections.forward: Ratih wants a proper place on the Freewind guard, rostered and briefed and part of a line instead of a woman alone on the salt. She's asked twice, and both answers were polite. She's going to ask a third time. She's already decided what she'll say if the answer is the same.

recruits.look: Indonesian woman in her late 30s, slim and weathered, black hair in a tight braid, a direct unsmiling face, fine squint lines. Green and grey leathers with a quiver worn high, a long recurve bow. A brass river-gauge plate, stamped with marks, sewn flat onto her sleeve.

recruits.name: Kourosh Behzadi
recruits.backstory: Twelve years pricing mortality for an insurer in Tehran, the work of establishing, very carefully, how likely a thing is. He finds arcane magic restful by comparison, because for once the numbers hold still. He's calculated a figure he won't tell anybody. The refusal is cheerful rather than grim, and people find that worse.
recruits.greeting: I'll stand at the back and be extremely precise, if that's all right with you. Somebody in a group ought to be brave, and it was never going to be the actuary.

background_sections.before: Kourosh spent twelve years as an actuary for an insurance company in Tehran, working out how likely people were to die so the company could price their policies. His father had taught mathematics and died while Kourosh was still a student, so the numbers felt like something he'd inherited. His mother, Shirin, worked at a bank and had always wanted more for him. He phoned her every Friday evening, and every Friday she told him he was wasting a good mind on spreadsheets. He never argued, because part of him agreed with her.
background_sections.adjustment: He was halfway through a calculation, pencil in hand, when he found himself in the hills of Hillsbrad. The first thing he did was sit down on a rock and finish the sum, because stopping halfway felt worse than anything else that was happening. People who heard the story later called it brave, which annoys him. He says it was habit, and his hands just kept going while his head caught up. It took him most of a year to stop working out whether his mother had survived, and he's never told anyone the figure he came to.
background_sections.now: These days Kourosh lives in the Crystalline Underdark, where the crystal lattice bends arcane magic in ways nobody has managed to explain. He's trying to explain it. He takes measurements every day and writes everything down by hand in a stack of notebooks wrapped in oilcloth to keep them dry. He's on his last notebook, and the readings in it worry him. The lattice is changing slowly, and if his numbers are right it'll be dangerous to anyone living near it before long.
background_sections.forward: There's no journal to publish in and nobody waiting to read his work, but he keeps writing because someone ought to know. He's tried to explain what he's found to two people so far, and both of them changed the subject. He wants to finish the measurements at the heart of the lattice while there's still time to warn anyone. After that, he says, he might let himself think about something other than odds. Nobody who knows him believes that.

recruits.look: Iranian man in his late 30s, slender and slightly formal in his bearing, black hair neatly cut, close beard, a face that looks faintly amused at all times. Indigo and silver robes with precise geometric trim, a staff of nested rotating rings. A slim mechanical pencil, silver, clipped inside the collar of his robe.

recruits.name: Driss Alaoui
recruits.backstory: Twenty-eight years guiding caravans out of Zagora, across ground where a wrong turn costs a camel and a second wrong turn costs a man. He reads sand the way a sailor reads water. The spirits of the land here needed an introduction, and then settled into something he finds entirely familiar: a long relationship with a landscape that would kill him on a technicality.
recruits.greeting: Have some water first, please, and then we can talk about whatever you came here to say.

background_sections.before: Driss guided camel caravans out of Zagora, in southern Morocco, for twenty-eight years, across ground where one wrong turn costs a camel and a second costs a man. He walked the same route his father and his grandfather had walked before him. He reads sand the way a sailor reads water. With his wife Khadija he raised four children on that work. Three of them were grown, and the youngest, Nour, was nine.
background_sections.adjustment: When he arrived, he asked the land for permission in his own language, and something answered him. He rarely mentions it. The rest of his adjustment was practical, learning new stars and new seasons and spending a year getting the distances right. The spirits here needed an introduction, and then they settled into something he finds very familiar, a long relationship with a landscape that would happily kill him.
background_sections.now: He's based at Freewind Post, between caravan runs across the canyons of Thousand Needles and the Shimmering Flats. The goblins pay well for a man who gets their cargo across intact, and he always does. He's turned down two contracts over the water allowance, and both times the other side came back with a better offer. A caravan that goes out with Driss comes back, and every trader in the canyons knows it.
background_sections.forward: Driss wants a route across the Shimmering Flats that a caravan can use in summer, when nobody can cross at all. He's sure there's a way through, and he's found most of it. Finishing it will take four more seasons of walking, and he has the seasons. He doesn't talk about Nour, but he carries a small wooden camel she carved for him.

recruits.look: Moroccan man in his mid 40s, lean and long-limbed, black hair greying at the temples under a wrapped headscarf, a narrow thoughtful face. Blue-grey mail and layered cloth with a totem stave and a horn at his belt, static lifting the loose ends of the scarf. A torque wrench, short and stubby, slung in a loop at his hip.

recruits.name: Marisol Quintero
recruits.backstory: Nine years in a Bogotá emergency department, three of them on nights, all of them short-staffed. She learned to keep a frightened person talking while her hands did something they'd rather not watch. The Light and the shadow both move through her easily, and she treats them as instruments on a tray. The habit of narrating came with her, and half the party finds it steadying and half find it maddening.
recruits.greeting: Talk to me while I work, about anything. I do better with a voice in the room, and so do you.

background_sections.before: Marisol spent nine years working in an emergency department in Bogota, three of them on nights and all of them short-staffed. She learned to keep a frightened person talking while her hands did something they'd rather not watch. Her brother Andres was a motorcycle courier in the same city, and she patched him up twice. The second time she shouted at him in the corridor for ten minutes, and she'd give anything to have that back.
background_sections.adjustment: She worked flat out for eighteen months, and she'll tell you honestly that she did it to stay out of her own head. It worked, and she'd do it again, and she knows exactly what it was. Both the Light and the shadow move through her easily, and she treats them like instruments laid out on a tray. She still talks people through what she's doing, the way she always did, and half the party finds it steadying and the other half find it maddening.
background_sections.now: She works out of the Sepulcher in Silverpine North, along the forest road where wolves and worse attack travellers, and the Forsaken garrison takes its time getting to them. Marisol gets to them faster. The garrison has noticed. The quartermaster, apparently, hasn't.
background_sections.forward: Marisol wants a proper ward, with four beds and a roof, where an injured person can lie down for a week instead of being patched up in a field. There's an empty building at the Sepulcher that would do. She's been negotiating for it for eleven months with a Forsaken quartermaster who keeps asking whose authority she's under. She's started to enjoy the arguments.

recruits.look: Colombian woman in her mid 40s, small and very upright, black hair in a severe low bun, a composed face that reveals nothing at all. Deep violet and black robes with a plain white collar, a slim dark staff, shadow pooling at the hem. A pair of folding reading glasses in a hard case, carried in one sleeve.

recruits.name: Diego Salazar
recruits.backstory: He fixed phones in a mall kiosk in Maracaibo from the age of fifteen, where the power went off twice a day and everybody learned to work in the dark. He can take a thing apart faster than he can explain why. He's one of the few people here who'll say plainly that this world has been good to him, and he won't apologise for it, because the one he left had stopped having anything for him.
recruits.greeting: Ah, you have a broken thing! Give it, give it. No, I'm not guessing, I can hear it. It's the same sound every time, my friend.

background_sections.before: Diego fixed phones at a kiosk in a shopping centre in Maracaibo from the age of fifteen, working at a folding table with a tray of screws while the power went off twice a day. He learned to work in the dark, and he can take a thing apart faster than he can explain why. His four older sisters all left Venezuela in different years and in different directions. He was the one who stayed to look after their mother, and he was twenty-two when she died, eight months before the Integration.
background_sections.adjustment: He settled in within three weeks and spent two of them delighted. A goblin handed him a broken pressure valve to see what he'd do with it, which is how a goblin asks a question. Diego had it working before the goblin finished his sentence, and he's been paid in parts ever since. He's one of the few people who'll tell you plainly that this world has been good to him. He won't apologise for it, because the one he left had stopped having anything for him.
background_sections.forward: Diego wants a workshop with his name over the door, and he can describe the sign exactly, in two colours, with the lettering slightly crooked because he likes it that way. He's twenty-five, and nobody has ever talked him out of anything. He won't argue with you about it. He'll smile, say sure, sure, my friend, and then do it his way.
background_sections.now: You'll find him wherever there's a pile of broken machinery and somebody willing to let him near it. He's been building a clockwork beetle for eleven months, and it's been nearly finished for all of them. Everyone who travels with him has been shown it. Nobody has ever seen it move.

recruits.look: Venezuelan man in his mid 20s, lean and wiry with quick hands, thick black hair falling over his forehead, dark eyes and a sharp jaw, a bright open good-looking face. Brass-and-canvas tinker's gear, a heavy wrench-hammer at his hip, goggles pushed up on his head. A phone-repair spudger, bright blue plastic scuffed white at the tip, in his breast pocket.

recruits.name: Freja Lindqvist
recruits.backstory: A midwife in Aarhus for six years, mostly nights. The job is being the calmest person in a room where something enormous is happening. She's blunt, and people find it a relief inside about a minute. She's also playful, competitive about everything, and she doesn't back down from anyone. The Light came to her easily and she treats it as a tool, the same as her hands, and she's careful to say so, because she's met two people here who decided they were chosen and she told both of them what she thought of that.
recruits.greeting: You're bleeding and talking at the same time, and you can only do one of those well. Sit down and I'll tell you when you're allowed to start again.

background_sections.before: Freja was a midwife in Aarhus for six years, mostly on nights, being the calmest person in a room where something enormous was happening. She rode her bicycle in every weather and lived in a flat with too many plants in it. One winter an American aircraft mechanic called William came off his bicycle on the ice outside her hospital. She strapped his wrist on the pavement and told him Americans shouldn't be allowed bicycles, and he told her Danes shouldn't be allowed opinions. They married two years later and argued happily about everything.
background_sections.adjustment: From the outside she seemed steady from the very first week. What she had was a working pair of hands and a world full of people who needed them, and she held onto that the way you hold a railing. She knows exactly what she was doing, and she'd do it again, and she wouldn't recommend it to anyone. The Light came to her easily, and she treats it as a tool, just like her hands.
background_sections.forward: Freja wants to deliver a baby on this world. She's told three people that, and watched all three fail to understand why it matters so much to her. Six years of her life were about the first ninety seconds of somebody else's, and she wants to know if that still means something here. She writes William a letter every week and keeps them in a bundle, because she's sure he'll read every one.
background_sections.now: She walks a circuit of the farms and camps around the Valley of Trials, because the fighting always gets a healer and the births get whoever happens to be nearest. She's taught four women to do what she does when she isn't there. That's the part of her work she's proudest of, and it's the part nobody ever asks about. She's blunt, competitive about everything, and people find her a relief within about a minute.

recruits.look: Danish woman in her late 20s, tall and slim with a dancer's posture, long pale blonde hair braided back, grey-blue eyes, fine straight features. White and soft-gold priest robes with a pale blue mantle, a slim silver censer at the belt. A midwife's wooden pinard horn, polished dark with handling, at her side.

recruits.name: Sondre Haugen
recruits.backstory: He taught sailing to teenagers on the Hardangerfjord for four summers and expected to do a fifth. He's good with weather and good with boats, and he was twenty-four and had never had anything bad happen to him. Then the sky here started answering when he spoke to it, and the first time it went wrong it went very wrong, and he's been frightened of himself ever since. He's polite about it, but you can still see it.
recruits.greeting: If I say get down, you get down and you ask me why afterwards. The asking is the part that kills people, and I've seen it happen.

background_sections.before:
A dinghy, a whistle, a clipboard, and a season that ended in August.

His parents and his sister Ingrid are in Bergen, and he has no idea if that means anything now. He talks about them in the present tense, every time, on purpose, like a man holding a door open with his foot.
background_sections.adjustment:
He'll tell you the first year was fine. Anybody who was there will tell you it wasn't.

One afternoon in the second year the wind did something he hadn't asked for, and a barn went over with people inside. Nobody was killed. A girl of about fifteen broke her leg, and he carried her out himself. He hasn't been the same since, and he can't explain why, when nobody died.
background_sections.forward:
Control, and not power. He's got plenty of power, and that's the whole problem.

He's started going out alone to practise where there's nothing to break. The people who care about him think that's the worst possible way to handle it, and they're probably right.
background_sections.now:
The high open ground near the Scarlet Crypt, where he can see weather coming for an hour before it arrives.

He sleeps badly. He's first awake every morning and he's made the fire before anybody else is up, and he offers that as proof he's fine.

recruits.look: Norwegian man in his late 20s, tall and rangy with broad flat shoulders, dark blond hair pushed back and wind-wrecked, pale grey eyes, a weather-reddened face. Storm-blue layered robes with a short cloak that lifts on its own, a long bone-white stave, faint static along his forearms. A sailing-dinghy shackle key on a lanyard at his throat.

recruits.name: Berat Yilmaz
recruits.backstory: A dentist in Izmir, newly qualified, still paying for the chair when the world changed under him. The job is small careful work inside a space the size of a fist, on somebody who'd rather be anywhere else. That turns out to be most of what field medicine asks for. He's wonderful company and he knows it and he uses it, because a frightened patient is a patient who moves.
recruits.greeting: Open wide, please. No, no, I'm joking, it's an old habit from the surgery. Sit down and let me have a look at that arm.

background_sections.before: Berat grew up in Izmir, in a building on the north side of the bay where three generations of Yilmazes lived on four floors and all talked at once. His father sold carpets, his mother ran everything, and he had three older brothers, every one of them louder than him. He was the first in the family to go to university, and his grandmother told the whole street. He'd had his own dental surgery for eleven months, with his name on the door and a loan with thirty years left to pay.
background_sections.adjustment: He was halfway through a filling, with his mouth mirror tucked behind his ear, when the patient and the chair vanished and he was standing in a field outside Brill. It took him about two months to settle, and most of that was learning the language. He had better hands than almost anyone and no idea what to do with the rest of himself. So he started asking everyone he met what they used to do, and he now remembers the old jobs of about four hundred people.
background_sections.forward: Berat wants a proper surgery again, with a door and his name on it, and an apprentice who isn't frightened of anything. He's also keeping a list of everyone from Earth with medical training, because he noticed early on that nobody else was, and it's now the only list like it. He says every day that he'll find his family. He says it like something he's decided to believe, because he doesn't know what happens if he stops.
background_sections.now: He works wherever the road is busiest, because that's where the broken arms are, and he sleeps in Brill when he sleeps at all. Small, careful work in a tight space on someone who'd rather be anywhere else turns out to be most of what field medicine is. He's wonderful company and he knows it, and he uses it, because a frightened patient is a patient who moves. He still keeps the mirror behind his ear, and mostly uses it to see round corners.

recruits.look: Turkish man in his late 20s, compact and sturdy, dark curls cut close at the sides, heavy black brows, warm brown eyes, an open face that smiles easily. Copper-plated tinker's coat in oxblood and brass, a backpack of tubes and gauges leaking soft green healing light. A dentist's angled chrome mouth mirror tucked behind one ear.

recruits.name: Matías Fuentes
recruits.backstory: He worked the buses in Chile's capital from nineteen, punching tickets on a route he could have driven blindfolded, in a job his father had before him and thought was beneath his sons. What he's good at is standing still in a crowd of strangers for nine hours and watching all of them at once. He speaks carefully and not much, in English he's built from nothing in three years, and people mistake that for stupidity about twice before they stop.
recruits.greeting: I go in front, because it's better that way. You can talk to me afterwards if you want to, but now isn't the time for talking.

background_sections.before: Matias worked the buses in Santiago from the age of nineteen, punching tickets on a route he could have driven blindfolded. His father had the same job before him and thought it was beneath his sons. What Matias was good at was standing still in a crowd of strangers for nine hours and watching all of them at once. His father died in 2019, and they hadn't spoken for two years. His mother and his little brother were at home when everything changed.
background_sections.adjustment: He'll tell you plainly that it went badly, if you ask him directly, and almost nobody does. He stopped speaking for most of his first year without meaning to. He ran out of things worth the effort of translating, and the quiet got comfortable, and then it got hard to leave. He's built his English from nothing in three years. People mistake his care with words for slowness about twice, and then they stop.
background_sections.forward: Matias is learning to read this world's script, slowly, from a woman at a trading post in Durotar who charges him nothing and corrects him constantly. He hasn't told anybody why. He wants to write a letter to his mother. He knows there's nowhere to send it, and he wants to write it anyway.
background_sections.now: He fights at the front, in the Sunken Grotto of the Deep or anywhere else that's dark, because from there he can see everyone. He clicks his old ticket punch twice before every fight. Somebody once asked him if it was for luck, and he said no and didn't explain. He's only ever told one person about his family, at night, on watch.

recruits.look: Chilean man in his late 20s, slim and hard through the shoulders, black hair worn a little long and shoved back, dark eyes, high cheekbones. Charcoal and bone-grey reaper leathers with a hooded half-cape, a long curved scythe-blade carried low, faint violet light at the edge. A bus conductor's brass ticket punch on a cord at his belt.

recruits.name: Giorgi Beridze
recruits.backstory: Twenty years of high summer pasture above Kazbegi, moving sheep up and down a mountain on a calendar his family never wrote down because nobody needed to. He's physically enormous and completely unhurried. His English has grown in three years and he still spends it like money, every word deliberate, and what comes out is often better than what a fluent man would say, because he's got no spare words to hide behind.
recruits.greeting: You walk too fast for this ground, so go slowly. The mountain will wait for you, and you'll learn to wait for it, if you listen.

background_sections.before: Giorgi spent twenty years on the high summer pastures above Kazbegi, in Georgia, moving sheep up and down the mountain on a calendar his family never wrote down because nobody needed to. He lived in a wooden hut with a dog and a herd, six months a year without a road. His wife Nino and their two daughters lived in the village below, and he came down to them every autumn. They thought the mountain was an eccentricity he'd grow out of, and he never did.
background_sections.adjustment: He says it took him two seasons to settle, because he counts in seasons. The land here needed reading, and he reads land, so that part was easy. People took longer. On the mountain he spoke to nobody for weeks and that was normal, but here other people worry about him when he's alone. He finds that exhausting and touching at the same time.
background_sections.forward: Giorgi wants a herd of his own again. He means it seriously, and nobody takes him seriously, and that irritates him more than he lets on. He's found grazing here as good as anything at home. He's also found a tauren herder who argues with him about it constantly, and he enjoys that enormously.
background_sections.now: He lives on the high ground above Tarren Mill, where the air is right and the ground tells the truth. His English has grown over three years, but he still spends it like money, every word deliberate. Every autumn, on roughly the right day, he walks down to lower ground for no reason anyone can see. He's bringing the herd down, and there's no herd.

recruits.look: Georgian man in his mid 30s, big through the chest with heavy forearms, thick dark hair and a short full beard, deep-set hazel eyes. Green and tan hide over mail, a hand-carved totem stave across his back, a hawk's feather bound into it. A shepherd's small dented brass bell, knotted to his belt so it cannot ring.

recruits.name: Camille Roussel
recruits.backstory: For nine years she raced packages across Lyon on a bike, and fixed every other courier's bike too. The job is knowing exactly how much space you have and taking all of it. She's abrasive on purpose, fast, and very funny when she decides to be, and almost nobody gets past the first layer. The ones who do find out she's fiercely loyal, and she'd deny it to your face.
recruits.greeting: If you want me along, that's fine. But I don't do the thing where we all talk about our feelings round the fire, so if you can live with that, we'll get on.

background_sections.before: Camille spent nine years as a bike courier in Lyon, racing packages across the city and fixing every other courier's bike as well. She rode a fixed-gear frame she'd built herself, twice, and she could cross the whole city in twenty-two minutes. The job was knowing exactly how much space she had and taking all of it. Her brother Theo rode for the same company. On the morning everything changed, he was out on the Part-Dieu road and she wasn't, because she'd swapped a shift so she could sleep in.
background_sections.adjustment: She made herself useful straight away and didn't let anyone near her for two years. It worked, in the sense that she survived it, and she knows it wasn't the only way she could have done it. She says the other ways were for people with more patience than her. She's mentioned the shift she swapped out loud exactly twice, and she regretted it both times.
background_sections.forward: Camille is mapping every road between the camps by hand, by riding them herself. If you ask her why, she says somebody ought to. The real answer is that it's the only thing here that feels like her old job, and that job was the last part of her life that worked. She'd deny every word of this to your face.
background_sections.now: She spends most of her time on the roads, carrying things between camps faster than they've any right to arrive. Lately she's been mapping the tunnels of the Wailing Caverns too, where nobody else has bothered. She won't carry a message she hasn't read, because she learned the hard way in her second month what that can cost. She's abrasive on purpose, and the few people who get past it find out she's fiercely loyal.

recruits.look: French woman in her early 30s, slim and long-legged, dark brown hair in a thick loose plait over one shoulder, green eyes, elegant features and a faint knowing half-smile. Deep green and oxblood brigand leathers cut close, a hooded short cloak, a long dagger at the hip. A slim silver bicycle-spoke wrench threaded onto her belt.

recruits.name: Orlando Rivera
recruits.backstory: Eleven years cutting hair in Santurce, in a shop that was really the whole neighbourhood's living room. Everybody told him everything, because a barber is a priest with better gossip. He talks constantly and listens harder than anybody notices. The spirits took to him straight away, and he treats them the way he treated his chair. Sit down, tell me what's wrong, and we'll talk the whole time I fix it.
recruits.greeting: Sit down, sit down, you look terrible, my friend, and I say that with love. Tell me what's wrong while I fix it.

background_sections.before: Orlando cut hair in Santurce, in San Juan, for eleven years, in a shop that was really the whole neighbourhood's living room. He had two chairs and a radio that was always on. A regular called Don Beni came in every Tuesday for nineteen years and never once needed a haircut. Everybody told Orlando everything, because a barber is a priest with better gossip. He talked constantly and listened harder than anyone noticed.
background_sections.adjustment: Within a month he was running a chair in a tent with a borrowed razor. It was the most effective adjustment anyone made, and the reason was simple. Everything good in his old life had come from a room where people sat down and talked, so he built that room here before he worried about anything else. The spirits took to him straight away, and he treats them the way he treated his customers.
background_sections.forward: Orlando wants a proper shop, with a floor and a mirror. He has the razor, and he's had three offers of a building. He's turned all three down and can't explain why to anybody, including himself. His hands shook when he said no to the last one.
background_sections.now: He lives at the Shadowpine Altar on Fenris Isle, where the trolls taught him the spirits and let him keep a chair by the fire. Wherever the party stops becomes a barber's shop for as long as they're there. He'll cut anybody's hair, any race, for free, and nobody's ever refused him twice. His whole family was on the island back home, and he says they're fine, for a reason that's thin, and everybody lets him have it.

recruits.look: Puerto Rican man in his early 30s, broad-shouldered and trim, black hair in a short fade, warm brown skin, an easy infectious grin. Bone and indigo witch doctor's gear, feathers and carved charms at the shoulder, a mask pushed up onto his forehead, a gourd rattle at his belt. A barber's pearl-handled straight razor in a sleeve pocket.

recruits.name: Adrián Mendoza
recruits.backstory: A football referee in the Segunda División for eight years, and before that a PE teacher. Two careers of being the least popular person on a field full of people. He is formal, exact and genuinely kind, and the formality is armour he put on so young that he has stopped noticing it. Give him a rule and he will hold it against everybody including himself, and he is the only man in any party who will tell you honestly when you were in the wrong.
recruits.greeting: Tell me the plan once, properly, and I won't need to ask again. I'm not being difficult, I promise. I'm trying to be useful.

background_sections.before: Adrian refereed football in Spain's second division for twelve years, and before that he spent nine years in the regional leagues, which he'll tell you were harder. He lived in Valladolid in a flat above a bicycle shop, and the noise never bothered him. His parents died within a year of each other when he was twenty-eight, and he had no brothers or sisters. Because he worked every Saturday and half of every Sunday, his friendships slowly thinned out, and he never chased them. He tells you all this as if he were reading out a team sheet.
background_sections.adjustment: He was useful within a week, which embarrassed him. The first thing he did here was reorganise a supply tent nobody had asked him to touch, and the second was argue with the quartermaster about it for twenty minutes. He won, and he's been winning small arguments like that ever since without apologising for any of them. What he still can't get used to is being wanted in a room. As a referee, if he did the job well, nobody said his name all afternoon.
background_sections.now: These days he holds the front line, which turns out to be close enough to his old job that he was good at it straight away. He gives the plan once, and if you make him repeat it he will, but he won't be pleasant about it. Tarek has pointed out that he could simply be nicer, and Adrian agreed that he could and carried on exactly as before. He still carries his whistle in his left pocket and pats it when he's thinking. He's never blown it here.
background_sections.forward: What Adrian wants, though he'd never say it, is to feel invited. People fetch him for meals, for the watch and for Ama's card game, and he goes every time and enjoys himself. But in three years he has never once walked up to a fire and sat down without someone waving him over first. If you asked him why, he'd say he doesn't want to intrude, and he'd believe it.

recruits.look: Spanish man in his early 30s, tall and square-shouldered, black hair cut short, close dark beard, a strong jaw. Polished steel and ivory templar plate with a deep red tabard, a one-handed sword and a shield at his back, faint gold light at the seams. A referee's whistle on a black lanyard inside the collar.

recruits.name: Saoirse Ni Bhraonain
recruits.backstory: She played county camogie until her knee went at twenty-six, and then she coached it. The sport is running at people holding a stick and expecting to be run at in return. She's loud, funny and completely without self-pity, and she has an instinct for getting in front of things that predates any of this. Of all of them she's the one most people would want beside them, and she'd find that embarrassing and change the subject.
recruits.greeting: Get behind me and stay there. I know, I know, you're very capable. Humour me and we'll both be alive to argue about it later.

background_sections.before:
A pitch in Kilkenny, a knee that clicked, and a minibus full of fifteen-year-olds she drove to matches at seven in the morning.

No partner, no children, two parents who died within a year of each other, and a brother in Australia she spoke to twice a year out of habit. The girls on the team are the ones she thinks about. She was driving eleven of them to an away match when it happened.
background_sections.adjustment:
Easy, and she's a little ashamed of how easy.

She arrived in a world that wanted somebody to stand in front, and standing in front is the only thing she's ever been unambiguously good at. She's watched people far better than her fall apart while she got on with it, and she has no explanation and offers none.
background_sections.forward:
To coach again, and not to fight.

She's started with four of the youngest at the Sepulcher, teenagers from Earth, on the grounds that somebody has to teach them to fall properly. She runs it at seven in the morning, because that's apparently who she is.
background_sections.now:
The Sepulcher in Silverpine, and Shadowfang Keep wherever the line's thinnest, taking the hits with a cheerfulness other people find unsettling.

The sliotar is still on her belt. She throws it at people who are getting above themselves, underarm and accurately, and the party has learned to catch.

recruits.look: Irish woman in her early 30s, tall and strongly built, long copper-red hair tied back in a heavy knot, pale freckled skin, grey-green eyes. Silver and midnight-blue plate, a round shield with a crescent boss, a short spear, cold moonlight along the armour edges. A hurling sliotar, scuffed and grass-stained, in a net at her belt.

recruits.name: Nicolás Arce
recruits.backstory: Nine years a paramedic in Lima, mostly on motorbikes, because an ambulance can't get through that traffic and a bike can. The work is triage at speed with your hands in somebody's blood, and blood magic asked him for exactly that with the pretence removed. He's steady, unhurried and very hard to frighten, and the one thing that will shut him down completely is being told to leave somebody behind.
recruits.greeting: Stand behind me, and if I go down, you run, and you don't try to drag me. Promise me that now, or find somebody else.

background_sections.before: Nicolas spent nine years as a paramedic in Lima, mostly on motorbikes, because an ambulance can't get through that traffic and a bike can. The work was triage at speed, with his hands in somebody's blood. For six years his partner on the bike was Gladys Huaman, who trained him and swore at him constantly. She was two streets away when everything changed.
background_sections.adjustment: He worked, and that's his entire answer, and he gives it in exactly those words. Blood magic asked him for the same thing his old job did, without any pretending. His second year was worse than the first, because by then he'd run out of nearby places to look for Gladys. He had to accept that finding her was going to be a long project rather than a short one.
background_sections.forward: Nicolas wants to find Gladys first of all, and he won't pretend otherwise or make anyone else carry it. He keeps a list of every town he hasn't reached yet. Beyond that he wants a crew, two people on something fast, heading towards what everybody else is running from. He hasn't found the second person.
background_sections.now: He's at Splintertree Post in Ashenvale East, at the front of whatever party he's in, soaking up what's aimed at the people behind him. He's steady, unhurried and very hard to frighten. He's the one who notices an hour before anybody else that somebody isn't right. He doesn't announce it, he just ends up walking beside them.

recruits.look: Peruvian man in his early 30s, compact and visibly strong, black hair swept back, dark eyes, high cheekbones. Crimson and black plate worn heavy, a broad shield, a short thick blade, dull red light moving under the plate like something circulating. A paramedic's folding tourniquet windlass clipped at his shoulder.

recruits.name: Ileana Dragomir
recruits.backstory: Second violin in the Cluj philharmonic for eleven years. The job is being corrected in public by a man with a stick, and then doing it exactly right forever after. She's scathing about anything done carelessly and has no patience at all for effort without precision. She's also the first on her feet when somebody goes down, every time, without comment, and the party works that out long before she admits it.
recruits.greeting: That was sloppy, and you know it was. Do it again properly and I'll stop talking about it, probably.

background_sections.before: Ileana played second violin in the Cluj philharmonic for eleven years, a job that meant being corrected in public by a man with a stick and then getting it exactly right forever after. Her husband Andrei taught at the conservatory. They'd decided together not to have children, and both of them had quietly wondered about it since. They'd just had a bad year and were coming out the other side of it. She'll describe the bad year in detail, but she can only say the last part once.
background_sections.adjustment: By her own account, she was unbearable for two years, and she says so flatly. She drove people away and knew she was doing it while she did it. She's since apologised to four of them, one at a time, and been surprised every time that they accepted. She's precise about her own faults in a way almost nobody is.
background_sections.forward: Ileana wants an ensemble rather than an audience, three or four people who can hold a line while she holds hers. She said this once, in a way that made it clear she meant the party. Then she immediately criticised somebody's footwork so that nobody could answer her. Nobody has asked her about the violin twice.
background_sections.now: She works the Plague Depths below the Undercity, where the cold suits her and the dead are a problem that needs precision. She stands at the back, and the front rank has learned to keep clear of the cold that comes off her. She's scathing about anything done carelessly. She's also the first on her feet when someone goes down, every time, without a word, and the party works that out long before she admits it. Her violin's shoulder rest is strapped across her back, though there's no violin.

recruits.look: Romanian woman in her mid 30s, slender and very upright, dark brown hair cut in a sharp chin-length bob, pale skin, dark eyes, fine sculpted features. Frost-white and deep grey robes with a high collar, a staff of pale bound bone, breath fogging and rime creeping along her sleeves. A violinist's black curved shoulder rest strapped flat across her back.

recruits.name: Thiago Macedo
recruits.backstory: A physiotherapist in Belo Horizonte who worked mostly with people recovering badly from accidents and strokes. The work is being relentlessly encouraging to somebody who wants to give up and is entitled to. He's huge, gentle and very hard to discourage. The Light came to him in the second year, and the people who know him best say it didn't change him at all, and he agrees, and finds that funny.
recruits.greeting: Hey, hey, look at me. You're not dying today. This I promise you, and I don't promise things.

background_sections.before:
A clinic, a table, and a schedule of people he saw twice a week for months at a time.

A huge family, all on three streets, all in and out of each other's houses. He talks about them constantly and in the present tense. Eleven months ago he saw a cousin's name, Júlio Macedo, on a list at a hub in the south, and he's been walking south in stages ever since, in no hurry, because he's decided it's certain.
background_sections.adjustment:
Eight months, and he spent them being useful to people in a way nobody had asked for.

He was the man who sat with people from Earth in the bad weeks, before anybody organised anything. He still is. He doesn't call it a vocation, and he gets uncomfortable when other people do.
background_sections.forward:
South, eventually, at his own pace, to Booty Bay where the list was.

He's also taught four people how to move an injured body without making it worse, because he watched somebody's back get broken twice: once by a boar and once by the people carrying him away from the boar.
background_sections.now:
Grom'gol, in Stranglethorn, on his way south. In the party he stands in the middle, where he can reach either end of it.

The roll of blue tape is nearly finished. He rations it. He's strapped three people's knees with it, and he'll tell you their names.

recruits.look: Brazilian man in his early 30s, tall and powerfully built, black curls cropped close, warm brown skin, a broad open face with a ready smile. Gold and white paladin plate worn light at the shoulder, a warhammer carried head-down, a soft gold glow around his gauntlets. A physiotherapist's half-used roll of bright blue kinesiology tape in a belt pouch.

recruits.name: Skye Donnelly
recruits.backstory: Eleven seasons with a Country Fire Authority brigade outside Ballarat. It's volunteer work that eats your entire summer and most of your friendships. She knows fire as a thing with moods, and she's the only caster most people have met who treats her own magic as something to be managed rather than owned. She's very funny and swears a great deal and is completely dependable at the moment it matters.
recruits.greeting: Right, stand upwind and don't touch anything that's glowing. That's the whole briefing, and you'll be fine.

background_sections.before:
A tanker, a pager, and a shed with a kettle in it where the crew sat out the nights nothing happened.

Divorced at twenty-nine, amicably, and she'll say the fire brigade was most of the reason and that she'd do it again. Her parents retired to Queensland. She assumes they're fine, on grounds she admits are entirely vibes.
background_sections.adjustment:
She found a fire in her first week and put it out, and says that sorted her head out for a year.

The harder part was finding out she could start one. She's thought about that more than she lets on, and she has a rule she tells nobody, and she's never broken it.
background_sections.forward:
A proper brigade. Actual volunteers, actual training, actual kit, for a world that burns constantly and has nobody organised about it.

She has six people. Four of them turn up. She describes this as going extremely well, and she means it.
background_sections.now:
Wherever the burning is, which in this world is most places. Lately that's the Drowning Floor under Southern Thousand Needles, where something keeps setting the oil seeps alight under the water. A pyromancer in a flooded cave makes everyone laugh, her included.

The helmet torch is still clipped to her belt and the battery died two and a half years ago. She clicks it on out of habit and laughs at herself every time.

recruits.look: Australian woman in her early 30s, athletic and sun-browned, long honey-blonde hair pulled up messily, light blue eyes, freckles. Scorched orange and ash robes cut short at the sleeve, a slim rod wrapped in blackened wire, heat shimmer off her forearms. A firefighter's yellow smoke-stained helmet torch clipped at her belt.

recruits.name: Vuk Jovanović
recruits.backstory: He ran a kafana in Novi Sad that his uncle left him, and he's a far better cook than he is a fighter. He says so himself, with some bitterness. He's blunt to the point of rudeness about small things and completely reliable about large ones. He took to this world badly and is only now coming out of it, and the coming out looks like him feeding people and insulting them while he does it.
recruits.greeting: You cooked this? I'm sorry, but it's terrible. Sit down, I'll show you. No, you sit, it's faster if I do it.

background_sections.before:
A kitchen, a card table, and forty regulars who came for the beans and stayed because there was nowhere else.

A daughter, Mila, who was nine, and an ex-wife, Jelena, he was on decent terms with. They had Mila on alternate weeks. It wasn't his week.
background_sections.adjustment:
Two years that he describes in three words, and nobody presses him on them.

What brought him back was being handed a cooking pot in a camp and being too irritated by how badly it was being used to leave it alone. He's cooked for whoever's nearby ever since, and he still says he isn't a cook any more.
background_sections.forward:
He won't say. He's been asked, and he changes the subject every time, usually to food.

What anyone can see is that he's started keeping a second bowl ready at every meal, without being able to say who he thinks it's for.
background_sections.now:
Rocky Pass, the cleft up to the summit of the Aspen country, at the front with an axe, badly, and at the fire afterwards doing the thing he's actually good at.

He carries a domino from the kafana set, the double six, in his glove. He puts it on the table when he sits down to eat. He's never explained it, and nobody asks.

recruits.look: Serbian man in his mid 30s, very tall and heavy-framed, dark hair shaved close at the sides, pale eyes, an old thin scar through one brow. Black and dull-iron war plate with a torn dark surcoat, a two-handed axe across his back, faint cold green light in the gorget. A cast-iron domino tile, double six, carried in one glove.

recruits.name: Khalid Al Suwaidi
recruits.backstory: He kept falcons outside Al Ain, in a family that had done it for longer than anybody wrote down, and he worked in logistics at the airport to pay for it. The hunting is the part of his old life that transferred whole: the waiting, the reading of ground, and the particular relationship with an animal that's choosing to come back to you. He's dry, extremely funny once you know him, and more at home here than he ever admits in company.
recruits.greeting: Walk where I walk and we'll have a very boring day. Boring is the aim, and I really can't stress that enough.

background_sections.before: Khalid kept falcons outside Al Ain, in a family that had done it for longer than anybody had written down, and he worked in logistics at the airport to pay for it. He'd flown a saker falcon called Hurra since she was a fledgling, eleven years. His large family all lived nearby, and they all thought the falcons were an expensive eccentricity. They came out to watch every time anyway.
background_sections.adjustment: He settled in within three months, and he has the grace to find that funny. He landed in open country full of weather and birds, with no airport anywhere. If he's honest, he says, the first year was the best he'd had in a decade. He only says it quietly, and only to people he trusts not to misunderstand.
background_sections.forward: Khalid wants a bird again, properly trained and properly flown, not a summoned thing. For two seasons he's been working, patiently and badly, with a nest of something enormous in the hills above the Flats. It's taken food from his hand twice. Both times it also tried to take the hand.
background_sections.now: He's based in Saltwheel, the goblin racing town on the edge of the Shimmering Flats. With a party he scouts ahead, usually out of sight and always exactly where he said he'd be. He's dry, and extremely funny once you know him. His old falconer's hood still hangs at his belt, sized for a bird he hasn't seen in three years.

recruits.look: Emirati man in his mid 30s, tall and lean, black hair under a loosely wrapped cloth headscarf, close beard, dark eyes, a hawkish face. Sand, grey and deep red survival leathers with a short cloak, a long recurve bow and a heavy belt knife, traps and cord at his hip. A falconer's small tooled leather hood hanging from his belt.

recruits.name: Karim Haddad
recruits.backstory: A land surveyor out of Amman, fifteen years of standing in empty country deciding where the lines went, mostly alone and entirely content with it. He took the fel deliberately, after consideration, as the fastest route to being useful in a fight, and he'll defend that choice in detail to anybody who raises it. He's cold on first meeting and very dry once he decides you're staying.
recruits.greeting: You're looking at my eyes, and everybody does. Either ask the question or stop looking, because either one is better than this.

background_sections.before: Karim was a land surveyor in Amman for fifteen years, standing in empty country with a tripod and a plumb bob, deciding where the lines should go. He spent weeks at a time alone and was perfectly content with it. He never married or had children, by choice. His parents had both died, and his brother Sami moved to Canada in 2011, and slowly they stopped calling each other. He tells you all this flatly, because he's noticed people want to be sad on his behalf, and he finds it tiring.
background_sections.adjustment: He treated this world as a survey, a new and unmapped country, and his whole trade was deciding where things are. He was working within a month. He'll tell you that having nobody to grieve made it easy, that he knows how that sounds, and that it's still true. He took the fel deliberately, after consideration, as the fastest way to be useful in a fight, and he'll defend that choice in detail.
background_sections.forward: Karim wants a real map of where people from Earth landed on this world, properly surveyed, and which places at home they came from. The pattern makes no sense, and nobody competent has looked at it. He's three years into a job that needs twenty, and he says so without minding. He's cold when you first meet him and very dry once he decides you're staying.
background_sections.now: He works in the Undercrust, beneath the Shimmering Flats, at the front of any party, where the green light from his eyes makes the people behind him uneasy. He's stopped apologising for it. The plumb bob still hangs at his hip, and he still uses it. The party has learned that when he stops and lets it swing, something ahead is wrong.

recruits.look: Jordanian man in his mid 30s, tall and lean-muscled, black hair cut short, close-trimmed beard, dark eyes with a faint green cast. Dark iron and fel-green plate with heavy pauldrons, a jagged greatsword across the back, green light bleeding from the joints. A surveyor's brass plumb bob on a worn cord at his hip.

recruits.name: Osvaldo Beltrán
recruits.backstory: He played trumpet in a Havana hotel band for sixteen years, six nights a week, for tourists who talked through all of it. He's enormously talented at a thing nobody here has any use for, and that's most of what's wrong with him. His English is better than he lets on, and he still uses as little of it as he can, and he's blunt to the point of rude and has never been unkind about anything that mattered.
recruits.greeting: If you want fire, I'll give you fire. If you want conversation, I'm the wrong man.

background_sections.before: Osvaldo played trumpet in a Havana hotel band for sixteen years, six nights a week, for tourists who talked through all of it. His brother Ruben played piano in the same band, and he was better than Osvaldo and knew it. Their mother was ninety-one and lived three streets from the hotel, and Osvaldo visited her every afternoon before the set. He's said one sentence about her in three years.
background_sections.adjustment: He stopped playing when he arrived, because there was nothing to play and nobody to play with. He put the trumpet down, and it stayed down. The fire came after that, and he'll tell you the order matters. He was already empty when he went looking for it, and he thinks that's the only reason it took.
background_sections.forward: Osvaldo won't admit to wanting anything. What anyone can see is that twice now he's stayed up all night with someone in a bad way, saying almost nothing, just sitting with them. Both of them told someone about it afterwards, and he denied it both times. Somebody heard him humming once, badly, and had the sense to say nothing.
background_sections.now: He's aboard the Bloodsail Raider, working as the pirates' hired fire, burning ships for people he doesn't care about, and he's tired of it. His English is better than he lets on, and he uses as little of it as he can. He's blunt to the point of rudeness, and he's never once been unkind about anything that mattered. His old trumpet mouthpiece hangs at his throat, and nobody has seen him use it.

recruits.look: Cuban man in his late 30s, broad-chested and thick-armed, black hair shaved close, warm brown skin, a heavy-browed face that rarely moves. Scorched black and ember-orange robes with the sleeves burned back, a staff capped in a slowly burning coal, soot on his hands. A trumpet mouthpiece, brass gone dull gold, on a cord round his neck.

recruits.name: Bashir Khalidi
recruits.backstory: A stonemason in Nablus for twenty-two years, in a trade of taking something apart correctly before you rebuild it. He's severe, literal and entirely without small talk, and people read that as coldness for about a week. He hunts corrupted things the way he cut stone: slowly, along the grain, with no interest at all in how long it takes.
recruits.greeting: I'll tell you what I find, all of it, including the parts you'd rather I kept to myself. If that's a problem, say so now.

background_sections.before: Bashir was a stonemason in Nablus for twenty-two years, working in the same yard where his grandfather and his father had cut stone. He learned the trade at twelve, and he still snaps a chalk line across every block before he cuts it, so the cut runs true. His wife Samira died giving birth to their second child when their daughter Rana was three, and the baby died too. He raised Rana alone and strictly. The week before everything changed, she told him she meant to study engineering, and he was proud but hadn't said so yet.
background_sections.adjustment: He went looking for Rana the moment he arrived and didn't stop for eleven months. He walked to four towns in that time, on foot, through country that kills people, and he found no trace of her. Then he came back, said nothing about it to anyone, and started the work he does now. He hunts corrupted things the way he used to cut stone, slowly, along the grain, with no interest in how long it takes.
background_sections.forward: Bashir keeps a list of every place he hasn't searched for Rana yet. The list is getting shorter, and he's started to look at what's waiting at the end of it. He's told one person that he means to be useful until then, and that's the whole of his plan. He's never said what he'll do if the list runs out.
background_sections.now: He works at the Drowned Shrine, off the coast of Southern Stranglethorn, out at the edge of the corruption with a lantern. The work is slow and dangerous, and almost nobody volunteers for it. He still snaps a chalk line across every doorway before he goes in, and he does it without seeming to notice. People take his bluntness for coldness for about a week, and then they learn he simply has no small talk.

recruits.look: Palestinian man in his early 40s, tall and spare with long hard forearms, black hair cut short and grey at the temples, a severe face with a strong nose. Black and bleached-bone leathers under a long storm coat, a heavy crossbow at the hip, a silvered blade, a lantern burning pale white. A stonemason's blue-dusted chalk line reel at his belt.

recruits.name: Gianluca Ferri
recruits.backstory: He ran a bar in Bologna that his parents ran before him, opening at six for the people going to work and closing late for the people avoiding going home. Thirty years of standing behind a counter reading a room. He talks without stopping, he remembers what everybody drinks, and he's defused more fights with a joke than most soldiers have with a weapon. Behind a shield he's immovable, and nobody expected that from the man who won't shut up.
recruits.greeting: You want to go in there? Fine, fine, but we go slowly, I go first, and afterwards you buy me something hot to drink. That's the arrangement.

background_sections.before: Gianluca ran a bar in Bologna that his parents had run before him, opening at six for the people on their way to work and closing late for the people avoiding going home. He spent thirty years behind that counter reading the room, and he rebuilt the coffee machine himself twice. The six o'clock crowd never had to order, because he already knew what they wanted. His wife Ornella ran the kitchen, the money and most of him. Their two grown sons lived in Milan and rang every Sunday.
background_sections.adjustment: Within four months he'd built himself a bar, or at least a spot by a fire where he stood and people came to him. He says he didn't know what else to do with himself. What he really missed was being the person everyone passes in the morning. Behind a shield he turned out to be immovable, which nobody expected from a man who never stops talking.
background_sections.forward: Gianluca wants a real bar, with a room, a door and a proper machine. He describes it constantly and in enormous detail, and in three years he hasn't done a single thing about it. Every few months he walks to the nearest town with lists of the missing. He reads the Bologna list first and then the Milan list, and he reads the Milan list twice.
background_sections.now: He keeps a fire at Steamwheedle Port where goblins, sailors and caravan guards come to him, and he remembers what every one of them drinks. In a fight he's at the front with a shield, keeping up a running commentary the enemy finds as unsettling as everyone else does. He's defused more fights with a joke than most soldiers have with a weapon. A brass coffee tamper hangs at his belt, though he has no coffee and no machine.

recruits.look: Italian man in his late 30s, broad and solidly built, dark hair greying at the temples, close beard, brown eyes, a lined face that looks faintly amused. Burnished bronze and deep blue plate, a kite shield, a short stabbing sword, a furled banner behind one shoulder. A barista's brass coffee tamper, handle worn smooth, at his belt.

recruits.name: Elias Peralta
recruits.backstory: A motorcycle mechanic in Santo Domingo who went to church on Sundays because his grandmother expected it, and stayed in the habit after she stopped being able to ask. He's the calmest person in most rooms. The Light arrived in his second year, during nothing in particular, while he was fixing a cart, and he's never presented it as a sign. He treats it as a tool that showed up, and he's been learning its tolerances ever since.
recruits.greeting: Take your time, hermano, I've got this side. Nothing's getting past me while you sort yourself out.

background_sections.before: Elias was a motorcycle mechanic in Santo Domingo, working under a tin roof with four bikes in pieces at any given time and a radio he and his cousin Junior argued over. He came from an enormous family in the capital. He went to church every Sunday because his grandmother expected it, and he kept going after she could no longer ask. He'd been seeing a girl called Yamila for two years and hadn't told his mother about her, for reasons that seemed important at the time.
background_sections.adjustment: His adjustment was slow and undramatic. He spent about eighteen months fixing things and let everything else wait. The Light came to him in his second year, while he was mending a cart, during nothing in particular, and he's never claimed it was a sign. He treats it as a tool that turned up, and he's been learning its limits ever since. He's said once that he doesn't think he's really dealt with any of it yet, and that it's still waiting for him somewhere.
background_sections.forward: Elias wants to build something that will outlast him, and he means a building, not a legacy. He's drawn up a shelter for a stretch of coast where travellers get caught out by storms, with four walls, a roof and a stove. He hasn't shown the drawing to anyone. He knows the first question will be who it's for, and he hasn't decided how to answer.
background_sections.now: These days he's at the Drownbell, on the coast of Northern Tanaris, and he stands at the front of any party, taking what's aimed at other people with an air of mild apology. He's the calmest person in most rooms. He keeps a mechanic's inspection mirror tucked in his gauntlet. He uses it to see round corners, and more often to check on the people behind him without turning round.

recruits.look: Dominican man in his early 30s, tall and lean with long limbs, black hair in a short twist-out, dark brown skin, warm dark eyes, a wide calm mouth. White and radiant gold plate with layered feathered pauldrons, a tall tower shield, light collecting above his shoulders. A mechanic's round telescoping inspection mirror in his gauntlet cuff.

recruits.name: Rui Almeida
recruits.backstory: He crewed a sardine boat out of Peniche from the age of sixteen, in a family trade that was collapsing under him the whole time he was in it. He's soft-spoken, apologetic and almost unbearably gentle, and he carries something that frightens him badly. He took it in his first year when the alternative was dying, and he's been paying for it since, and he's never tried to make it sound like a good decision.
recruits.greeting: Please don't ask me what it is. I'll tell you what it does, and that'll have to be enough, because the rest I can't say out loud.

background_sections.before: Rui crewed a sardine boat out of Peniche, in Portugal, from the age of sixteen, in a family trade that was collapsing under him the whole time. In his working life the fishing co-operative shrank from forty boats to nine. His mother and his two sisters lived in Peniche, and he was the one who sent the money home. He thinks about the money more than he thinks about them, and he's ashamed of that.
background_sections.adjustment: His arrival was a catastrophe. He landed alone on the Tanaris coast with a broken leg, and something offered to help him. He said yes, because the alternative was dying, and he's been paying for it ever since. He's never tried to make it sound like a good decision. When people assume the worst about him he lets them, because arguing would mean explaining, and explaining is the part he can't do.
background_sections.forward: Rui wants out, quietly, without anyone making a fuss about it. He's asked three priests and two shamans, carefully and in general terms, and nobody has given him an answer he believes. He keeps asking. It's the only thing he's stubborn about.
background_sections.now: He lives at the Lashings, on the coast of Northern Tanaris, as close to the sea as he can get. In a party he stays behind everyone, very effective and visibly uncomfortable about it. He's soft-spoken, apologetic and almost unbearably gentle. He always sleeps nearest the fire, and nobody has worked out that it isn't because of the cold.

recruits.look: Portuguese man in his mid 30s, slim and a little gaunt, dark hair worn loose to the jaw, deep-set dark eyes, hollow cheeks. Deep violet and black robes with a torn high collar, a thin crooked staff, shadow pooling and moving wrongly around his feet. A fisherman's salt-bleached wooden net needle through his belt.

recruits.name: Nizar Haddad
recruits.backstory: A mathematics teacher three times over, with eleven years in Homs, then six in Beirut, then four in Hamburg in a language he was still learning. He's rebuilt his life three times, and this is simply the fourth. He says so without any self-pity, and most people from Earth go quiet when they hear it. His English is careful and slightly old-fashioned, learned from books and the BBC, and he's more precise in it than most people born to it.
recruits.greeting: A moment, if you'd permit me. I should like to understand the sequence before we add ourselves to it.

background_sections.before: Nizar taught mathematics three times over, for eleven years in Homs, then six in Beirut, then four in Hamburg in a language he was still learning. He had the patience of a man who can explain the same proof for the ninth time without letting it show. His wife Lamia died in 2016, before any of the rest of it. His daughter Hala was twenty-two and studying in Amman, and they spoke every single day. He can tell you the exact time of their last call.
